governance_posts.title: 2025 Events Recap
governance_posts.description:
Greetings Aave Community,

We’re happy to publish this report with our events activity 2025, walking you through the activities we have organized and the results they yielded this year.

2025 has been a huge year for Aave, and we’re happy to report that the momentum and strength of the brand have come through in our live appearances. Our regular followers keep coming back for more, while we continue to add new partners to DeFi Day. For Cannes we welcomed four new sponsors into the community, and five out of the total twelve partners were onboarded for the Buenos Aires edition. We also captured the interest of existing and future integration partners, institutional targets and more.

The Aave brand strengthens every year and continues to be known for complementing the protocol’s growth, high-quality track record and lasting power. Buenos Aires was home to our rAAVE #13 and our fourth DeFi Day, and both events were sold out.

Cannes

We hosted two full days at a hillside villa with a wide view of the coast. It became home to meetings, our two flagship events (DeFi Day and rAAVE), and a V4 demo for the Aave DAO. The Aave villa was a standout during EthCC and became a destination on its own.

DeFi Summer Day

In Cannes, at DeFi Summer Day, attendance hit record numbers, with more than 2,600 people waitlisted and over 600 attending. Sponsors included Chainlink, Sky, Ethena, Etherfi, Certora, Chaos Labs, Aptos, ZKsync, Fireblocks, and more. Our panels picked up the pulse of the moment, covering stablecoins, RWAs, interop, and blockchain modularity. Speakers included Vitalik Buterin, Sergey Nazarov, Guy Young, Avery Ching, and many more.

The programming attracted partners from across the Aave ecosystem, ranging from crypto natives to institutional users, who were excited about the future of the Aave Protocol, Horizon, and GHO.

rAAVE Cannes

For rAAVE, we leaned into the Cannes vibe and turned the Aave villa into an all-white disco. The stage was set outdoors, with LED screens showing hand-drawn Ronnie animations. As usual, the door was packed, hitting capacity the entire night, and the energy was high.

We launched a new merch shop, this time featuring the coveted rAAVE pieces. A bar facing the ocean served cocktails, soft drinks, and wine. We watched the sunset from the deck to Max Menaged, who opened the night. The dancing carried on with Antdot’s tropical grooves, Alma Linda, and closing with an incredible combo, Jamiie b2b Xenobi. rAAVE Cannes was a success, drawing even media attention on CNBC.

The Cannes Merch Collection

Aave events wouldn’t be complete without custom, high-quality merch. For Cannes, we took inspiration from nautical elements from the French Riviera. We made embroidered t-shirts and linen pants, colorful polo shirts, and more. Crochet hats, fans, and totes were new additions for rAAVE, and the ultra-soft Aave and GHO socks made a comeback.

EthCC Booth and Talks

Aave has always made it a point to support Ethereum France, which has consistently given us speaking slots at the conference and backed the brand from early on. We had a booth for the first two days, where Aave Labs engineers and business development teams met with builders and community members, explored new opportunities, and gathered user feedback.

In addition to it, Stani got to introduce Aave v4 on the main stage, and later on Emilio offered a deep dive on the upcoming upgrade’s innovative architecture.

Ronnie Film Festival by Metamask

Aave was invited by Metamask to host a custom experience for the week. In collaboration with Metamask, we created the Ronnie Film Festival, a one-day event that took Aave friends on a journey with macaron tastings, helicopter rides, and more.

Guests filmed their day, spent together with Ronnie, the Aave mascot, and the best clips were chosen by a jury and awarded trophies, in true Cannes style.

The activation helped launch the Metamask Card and spotlight the successful Linea Aave market.

London

DAS London DeFi Brunch with Galaxy and Blockchain.com

In October, we hosted over 80 people at the Aave Labs office for a brunch co-hosted with Galaxy and Blockchain.com. DAS (Digital Asset Summit) gave us a strong moment to grow Aave’s presence across institutions and real-world assets.

Buenos Aires

Devconnect Argentina

Aave Labs took over the DeFi District at La Rural, the venue for Devconnect Argentina. As usual, the booth had lines throughout the week. We used the spotlight to announce the Aave app waitlist, powered by Aave V3, while keeping focus on V4 awareness and business development.

Our top engineers joined the event, along with a video team capturing interviews and content to grow our presence on Instagram and TikTok.

Across the six days of Devconnect, Aave Labs spokespeople appeared across multiple stages:

  • Stani shared the new Credit architecture at Ethereum Day, joined Manuel Beaudroit for a fireside chat at Crecimiento’s Startup World Cup, and spoke on stablecoins at the Ethereum Foundation’s DeFi Today.

  • Mario Baxter Cabrera (Director of Product) introduced the Aave App at the World Fair stage: DeFi’s “iPhone moment.”

  • Mark Hinschberger (Senior Engineering Manager) presented Aave Pro, the new web app coming to aave.com.

  • Dhairya Sethi (Staff Engineer, Smart Contracts) and Tomer Ganor (Security Lead at Certora) walked through Aave V4’s security blueprint at the DeFi Security Summit.

Buenos Aires was also a fertile ground for us to ramp up our marketing video strategy efforts: several months ago, we had already started deploying the Smart Money series on Aave’s Instagram and TikTok, as well as short clips from the Cannes DeFi Day talks. In Buenos Aires we recorded vox pops, deep dives into Argentinian economy and how stablecoins are helping people deal with inflation, interviews, and more. This footage is currently being edited and posted.

DeFi Day Del Sur

The fourth edition of our flagship event took place on November 19, 2025, at La Escondida de Palermo in Buenos Aires. This time, we aligned with Devconnect’s goal of cementing the city as the crypto capital of Latin America.

We invited the founders of Lemon, Belo, Ripio, and Sovra.io to share how they’re driving regional adoption. All but Sovra have integrated Aave, collectively reaching more than 9 million users across LATAM.

Integrations overview:

  • Lemon has used Aave since 2021, with 4 million users across Argentina, Peru, and Colombia.

  • Ripio integrated in 2022. Its products reach 25 million people across Latin America, with 4 million app users mainly in Argentina and Brazil.

  • Belo serves over 1.5 million users in 20 countries, with a strong presence in Argentina and Brazil.

We co-hosted the event with 1inch, CoW DAO, Uniswap, Optimism, Aptos, Avalanche, Chainlink, Sky, kpk, Chaos Labs, Upshift, and Linea. Over 600 guests joined panels on commerce, stablecoins, DeFi innovation, RWAs, and more. We also brought back the fan-favorite merch shop with caps, t-shirts, tote bags, and other items.

rAAVE Buenos Aires

rAAVE Buenos Aires lit up Palacio Alsina, drawing over 1000 guests for a full night of music and celebration. Custom LED visuals brought Ronnie, flowers, and psychedelic animations to life. The crowd danced to B2B sets from Max Menaged, Jamiie x Julya Karma and Gallivanter x Xinobi, and an electric live performance by Sinego.

The Aave brand strengthens every year and continues to be known for complementing the protocol’s growth, high-quality track record and lasting power. Buenos Aires was home to our rAAVE #13 and our fourth DeFi Day, and both events were sold out.

Cannes

We hosted two full days at a hillside villa with a wide view of the coast. It became home to meetings, our two flagship events (DeFi Day and rAAVE), and a V4 demo for the Aave DAO. The Aave villa was a standout during EthCC and became a destination on its own.

DeFi Summer Day

In Cannes, at DeFi Summer Day, attendance hit record numbers, with more than 2,600 people waitlisted and over 600 attending. Sponsors included Chainlink, Sky, Ethena, Etherfi, Certora, Chaos Labs, Aptos, ZKsync, Fireblocks, and more. Our panels picked up the pulse of the moment, covering stablecoins, RWAs, interop, and blockchain modularity. Speakers included Vitalik Buterin, Sergey Nazarov, Guy Young, Avery Ching, and many more.

The programming attracted partners from across the Aave ecosystem, ranging from crypto natives to institutional users, who were excited about the future of the Aave Protocol, Horizon, and GHO.

rAAVE Cannes

For rAAVE, we leaned into the Cannes vibe and turned the Aave villa into an all-white disco. The stage was set outdoors, with LED screens showing hand-drawn Ronnie animations. As usual, the door was packed, hitting capacity the entire night, and the energy was high.

governance_posts.title: [TEMP CHECK] Aave Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Program
governance_posts.description:
Author: AxieAur

Title: Aave Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Program

Date: 2026-04-07

Abstract:

Initiate and implement AAVE Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Mechanism. Create mechanism to share monthly AAVE protocol revenues with stakers of AAVE token who have been staking for 30 or more days. Start monthly revenue share at .25% of Aave protocol monthly revenues. Users will be able to claim revenues from frontend dashboard.

Motivation:

The intent of this initiative is multi-faceted:

  • Create direct and long-term alignment between AAVE’s protocol profitability and AAVE token investors

  • Encourage further staking of $AAVE, taking coins out of circulating and reducing available supply

  • The idea of earning cash yield is more attractive than earning tokens for many investors

  • Signal to market and investors owning $aave means owning a part of the protocol revenue. The amount isn’t as important as the philosophical direction and signal. Investors will want to own a piece of the revenues from the largest decentralized borrow/lend protocol in the world especially as we scale into securing trillions of dollars

  • Add new value lever to AAVE token that can be increased or decreased dynamically based on company position, market conditions, etc… to increase the value proposition for $aave holders. Implement now while things are slow

Specification:

Each month:

On the first day of each month, .25% of Aave’s monthly revenues are made claimable to stakers of $AAVE who have staked for over 30 days (claim proportionate to user’s staked AAVE > 30 days / total staked AAVE > 30 days)

aave monthly revenue * (.0025) * (user’s stkaave amt > 30 days / total stkaave amt > 30 days) = user’s share of monthly revenue

This program can work in tandem with buybacks and/or buybacks can be eliminated if appropriate. Both have their pros and cons, and may be appropriate in different situations. There may also be situations where it makes sense to use neither.

The percentage of distribution is very small by design due to Aave’s current growth stage. There are trillions of dollars of value to be captured, and growing into the trillions of dollars secured is the most important goal. It is important the vast majority revenues focus on growth.

1 out of 400 dollars earned shared with stakers leaves 99.75% of revenues to be used for growth. Revenues shared in today’s environment would be very small.

Next Steps:

  • Collect community feedback, conduct discussion, iron out technical implementation path if idea is well received

Copyright is open source on this proposal

governance_posts.title: Streaming yield for Aave depositors and app savers
governance_posts.description:
Hi Aave community,

This is Amin from Superfluid. Superfluid powers continuous settlement for tokenized markets and the agentic economy.

We’re exploring where Superfluid could add value to Aave. We think that as yield becomes commoditized, the cashflow experience can become a differentiator for some users. Most savers might make an initial decision based on the APY. But they might not build an ongoing habit around it.

Superfluid can make yield become a visible real-time stream. A stream of money arriving every second feels different to a balance that changes from time to time. That inbound stream representing the yield can be used as income or redirected to other products on the platform. Here is a live technical demo of streaming yield from a Morpho vault: SuperVault. More on streaming yield here.

Could streaming yield be a useful option for Aave depositors and Aave App Savings users?

Appreciate any feedback from the Aave community.

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Cap and IRM Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.09.18
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase the borrow cap for wstETH from 7,000 to 14,000.

Aave V3 Base:

  • Decrease Slope1 for WETH from 2.50% to 2.30%.
  • Increase the optimal utilization for WETH from 90.00% to 92.00%.

Aave V3 Mantle:

  • Increase the supply cap for USDe from 20,000,000 to 40,000,000.

Aave V3 X Layer:

  • Increase Slope1 for USDC from 4.00% to 4.50%.

Aave V3 Horizon:

  • Increase the supply cap for USCC from 5,600,000 to 7,500,000.

wstETH (Aave V3 Core)

wstETH sits at 99.4% borrow cap utilization on Aave V3 Core, with 6,956 borrowed against a cap of 7,000.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, September 18, 2026

The top wstETH borrowers have health factors between 1.00 and 4.17, with a median of 1.12, and most of the cohort is clustered below 1.15. The collateral backing the wstETH debt is predominantly weETH, and WETH rather than stablecoins, so the health factor’s stability tracks the wstETH-versus-ETH spread within a single correlated asset family.

Recommendation

The proposed cap of 14,000 is approximately 2.01x the current outstanding borrow, resulting in approximately 49.7% post-change cap utilization.

WETH (Aave V3 Base)

The proposed change lowers Slope1 to 2.30% and raises the optimal utilization to 92.00%, implementing the Risk Stewards September 2026 WETH interest rate adjustment on Base, as published by TokenLogic. The base rate and Slope2 are unchanged. At the current 82.4% utilization, the post-change variable borrow rate would be 2.06% APR, down from 2.29% under the current IRM.


Source: LlamaRisk, September 18, 2026

Withdrawal Liquidity at the Optimal Point

The optimal point sets how much of the supply remains available for withdrawal when the reserve is at its intended operating level. Moving it up by two percentage points converts exit liquidity into borrow capacity.

Instance Asset Supplied Borrowed Utilization Idle Liquidity
Aave V3 Base WETH 84,792 69,886 82.4% 14,906
Instance Asset Buffer at Optimal (current) Buffer at Optimal (new) Change Borrow Headroom to Optimal (current) Borrow Headroom to Optimal (new)
Aave V3 Base WETH 8,479 6,783 -1,696 6,426 8,122

The change adds 1,696 WETH of borrow capacity before Slope2 engages, raising the headroom to the optimal point from 6,426 to 8,122 WETH and reducing the withdrawal buffer by the same amount. The reserve currently operates 9.6% below the new optimal point, and the present idle liquidity of 14,906 WETH is 2.2x the post-change buffer at the optimal point.

USDe (Aave V3 Mantle)

USDe sits at 96.6% supply cap utilization on Aave V3 Mantle, with 19.3M supplied against a cap of 20M.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, September 18, 2026

The supplier base is concentrated, with the largest position holding approximately 68.6% of supply and the top three positions holding approximately 99.6% of supply. Three of the four top suppliers carry debt at health factors between 1.03 and 1.04, posting USDe alongside sUSDe as collateral under the Mantle stablecoin E-Mode categories and borrowing USDT0 against it. Given that USDe on Aave is priced via the USDT/USD feed, these positions are correlated, reducing the liquidation risk.

Recommendation

The proposed cap of 40,000,000 is approximately 2.07x the current outstanding supply, resulting in approximately 48.3% post-change cap utilization.

USDC (Aave V3 X Layer)

The proposed change raises Slope1 to 4.50%. Optimal utilization, the base rate, and Slope2 are unchanged, so the rate at the optimal point moves from 4.00% to 4.50% APR, and the rate at full utilization moves from 44.00% to 44.50% APR. At the current 1.0% utilization, the post-change variable borrow rate would be 0.05% APR, up from 0.04% under the current IRM.

The reserve stands at 102 USDC supplied against 1 USDC borrowed, so the change applies to a reserve with no material outstanding position.

USCC (Aave V3 Horizon)

USCC, the Superstate Crypto Carry Fund token, sits at 92.0% supply cap utilization on Aave V3 Horizon, with 5,149,882 supplied against a cap of 5,600,000.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, September 18, 2026

The supplier base is concentrated: the largest position holds approximately 59.6% of supply, the top three hold approximately 78.6%, and every top supplier carries debt with a health factor between 1.04 and 1.11, with a median of 1.06. The debt is entirely stablecoin, approximately 46.5M in RLUSD and approximately 9.6M in GHO, so health factor stability tracks the USCC price.

Recommendation

The proposed cap of 7,500,000 is approximately 1.46x the current outstanding supply, resulting in approximately 68.7% post-change cap utilization.

Specification

Aave V3 Horizon USCC 5,600,000 7,500,000
Instance Asset Current Borrow Cap Recommended Borrow Cap

Next Steps

We will move forward and implement these updates via the Risk Steward process. The implemented changes can be reviewed on the LlamaRisk Risk Stewards Dashboard.

governance_posts.title: [Risk Stewards] September 2026 - WETH Interest Rate Adjustment on Base
governance_posts.description:
title: [Risk Stewards] September 2026 - WETH Interest Rate Adjustment on Base

author: @TokenLogic

created: 2026-09-17

Summary

In August, WETH Slope1 was reduced to 2.20% on Ethereum Core, Arbitrum, and Optimism, while Base remained unchanged. This publication proposes two changes to the WETH interest rate curve on Aave V3 Base: reducing Slope1 from 2.50% to 2.30% and raising Uoptimal from 90% to 92%.

Motivation

Overview

WETH on Base is the second largest ETH borrowing market on Aave, with approximately 69K WETH ($171M) of variable debt against 85K WETH ($211M) of supply. Utilization held between 87% and 89% through late August and early September, then fell to 81% over the last two weeks: borrowers repaid roughly 7K WETH from the 76K peak of 22 August while deposits recovered from 82K to 85K. The variable borrow rate followed utilization down, from around 2.50% to 2.27% APY, against a Uoptimal of 90%.


WETH on Aave V3 Base: user deposits and active loans in WETH, daily, last 90 days. Source: TokenLogic dashboard.


WETH on Aave V3 Base: utilization against the 90% Uoptimal, daily, last 90 days. Source: TokenLogic dashboard.

Demand on Base is driven by leveraged staking strategies in the ETH correlated eModes. cbETH deposits have grown from approximately 3.1K to 45.7K tokens ($128M) since May 2026, supported by a borrow-side incentive campaign on the cbETH to WETH loop that continues to run. A further $107M of weETH, wstETH and wrsETH collateral sits on the market with no borrow incentive attached, relying on the organic borrow rate alone.


cbETH on Aave V3 Base: user deposits in cbETH, daily, last 90 days. Source: TokenLogic dashboard.

ETH Borrow Rate Update

After the August adjustment, the WETH borrow rate is 2.08% APY on Ethereum Core, 1.98% on Arbitrum and 1.98% on Ethereum Lido, against 2.29% on Base. A 20 bps reduction brings Base within 10 bps of the other markets, which matches the yield premium of its dominant collateral, cbETH, over stETH, reverses the utilization decline of the last three weeks, and lets utilization move back from its current 81% toward the 92% Uoptimal.

Market Supplied WETH Borrowed WETH Utilization Borrow APY Supply APY Slope1 Uoptimal
Ethereum Core 2,102K 1,765K 86.1% 2.08% 1.48% 2.20% 92%
Arbitrum 97.5K 55.4K 81.9% 1.98% 0.95% 2.20% 92%
Base 85.2K 69.3K 81.4% 2.29% 1.58% 2.50% 90%
Ethereum Lido 18.8K 15.8K 84.2% 1.98% 1.41% 2.14% 92%
Optimism 8.4K 5.7K 68.0% 1.68% 0.97% 2.20% 90%

cbETH currently yields 2.35% (2.37% on a 30-day average), weETH 2.32% and wstETH 2.25%. At a 2.29% borrow rate, a cbETH loop earns 6 bps per turn of leverage before incentives, a weETH loop 3 bps and a wstETH loop is negative. For comparison, on Ethereum Core the equivalent wstETH loop earns 17 bps per turn. Leveraged strategies cannot be expected to carry utilization from 81% to the Uoptimal at a rate equal to their yield. Repayments over the last three weeks, made while the borrow rate sat between 2.4% and 2.5%, are consistent with strategies unwinding once the rate moved above their collateral’s yield.

Setting the Slope1 just below the yield of the dominant collateral enables the market to clear near the Uoptimal. On Ethereum Core, the 2.20% Slope1 sits 3 bps under the stETH yield at the kink. On Base, 2.30% sits 2 bps under the cbETH yield. Revising Slope1 below 2.30% would forgo revenue and require broader implementation across other instances to ensure consistency across the liquidity market.

The borrow campaign on the cbETH to WETH loop adds approximately 20 bps to the borrower’s carry. With the cut, the same incentive creates a positive organic margin for the campaign’s participants, and the weETH, wstETH, and wrsETH strategies that receive no incentive move from a marginal or negative organic carry to a positive one. The largest wETH supplier holds 14% of the supply, with the top five holding 32%, against 7% and 26% on Ethereum Core, 7% and 15% on Arbitrum, and 55% and 73% on Ethereum Lido, which operates with a 92% Uoptimal configuration. On the debt side, the largest borrower holds 23%, the same share as on Ethereum Core. Supplier concentration on Base has declined in recent months and sits well within the range of markets already operating at 92%.


Share of each Aave V3 WETH market held by its largest supplying and borrowing addresses, balances as of 17 September 2026. Supplier and borrower counts include positions above $10 only.

At the Uoptimal, 8% of supply remains available for withdrawals: 6.8K WETH ($17M) at current supply with 92% utilisation, against 8.5K WETH at 90% utilisation. Over the last twelve months, only three days saw net supply outflows above 6.8K WETH, and two of them (18K WETH on 25 November 2025 and 18K WETH on 19 April 2026) exceed the buffer liquidity in the Reserve. Withdrawals of that relative size are absorbed through utilisation spikes above the Uoptimal, where loan repayments and users exit hastily during periods of market stress. In the last 90 days, utilisation has not exceeded 92%, and it only exceeded 90% during a single week starting 24 August.

With the Base, Slope1 and Uoptimal set at 0%, 2.30% and 92%, the Aave DAO’s revenue in ETH terms increases when utilisation exceeds 86%. At the 90% level the market operated at through early September, the supply APR is 16 bps higher than today and reserve revenue 10% higher; at the new 92% utilisation, the supply APR is 24 bps higher and reserve revenue 15% higher.

Scenario Utilization Borrow APR Supply APR Borrowed WETH Reserve revenue (WETH / yr)
Current, Slope1 2.50% 81.4% 2.26% 1.56% 69.3K 235
Slope1 2.30%, Uoptimal 92%, utilization unchanged 81.4% 2.03% 1.41% 69.3K 212
Slope1 2.30%, Uoptimal 92%, breakeven 85.8% 2.14% 1.56% 73.1K 235
Slope1 2.30%, Uoptimal 92%, at the previous Uoptimal 90.0% 2.25% 1.72% 76.7K 259
Slope1 2.30%, Uoptimal 92%, at Uoptimal 92.0% 2.30% 1.80% 78.4K 270

Slope2 remains at 8%, in line with Arbitrum, Optimism and Ethereum Lido. With the Uoptimal at 92%, the borrow rate at 95% utilization is 5.3% and at full utilization 10.3%, against 6.5% and 10.5% on the current curve. The spike above the Uoptimal on 24 August, when 10K WETH of supply left the market in a week and the rate briefly reached 4.1%, was withdrawal driven, and the curve above Uoptimal is not changed by this proposal.

Specification

The Risk Stewards will implement the following changes on Aave V3 Base. Both moves sit within the Risk Steward’s single-action limits (100 bps for Slope1, 300 bps for Uoptimal) and can be executed in one update.

Market Asset Parameter Current Proposed
Base WETH Slope1 2.50% 2.30%
Base WETH Uoptimal 90% 92%

governance_posts.title: The Literacy Barrier in DAO Governance: How Technical Complexity Excludes the Global South
governance_posts.description:
Context

This post is not about a specific proposal. It is about a pattern I have observed over years of DAO governance research and experienced personally.

I am sharing it here because Aave is one of the most important governance communities in DeFi. If this conversation can happen anywhere, it should happen here.

The Core Observation

DAO governance presents itself as open and decentralized. But in practice, two invisible filters determine whose voice carries weight:

1. Token Concentration
Governance power flows to whoever holds the most tokens. Early insiders and protocol teams accumulated tokens before most of the world knew these protocols existed. Communities across South Asia, Africa, and Latin America were never part of that early accumulation.

2. Technical Fluency
Risk proposals arrive as multi-page documents filled with LTV ratios, oracle thresholds, and slippage curves written to demonstrate expertise, not to inform the community. When the bar for “valid participation” requires understanding 40-parameter risk tables, most people quietly conclude they have nothing to say.

Together, these filters make exclusion feel like a personal failing not a structural problem.

Data as Armor

There is a difference between using data for transparency and using complexity to avoid accountability.

When a service provider exits abruptly without community consultation, without a public post-mortem, without explaining what conflict triggered the departure and the community’s only response is another technically dense proposal, that is not transparency. That is the appearance of rigor being used to move past uncomfortable questions.

The real governance questions require no PhD:

  • Who decided this?
  • Was there a conflict of interest?
  • What accountability exists for damages to ordinary users?
  • What changes will prevent this next time?

What I Experienced Personally

When I raised carefully researched questions about a powerful service provider on this forum, my comment was placed on a 24-hour hold. On separate occasions, posts were removed. Across multiple governance forums, I have faced holds lasting months.

The stated reason: my questions could “affect a billions-dollar protocol.”

A community member asking a researched governance question was considered a risk. Not the abrupt vendor exit. Not the wrongful liquidations. Not the damages to ordinary users.

The question was the problem.

That is not community protection. That is insider protection.

The Global South Is Not Absent — It’s Unwelcome

India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka hundreds of millions of people with genuine reason to care about decentralized finance are largely absent from governance. Not because they lack intelligence or interest. Because these systems were built by and optimized for a specific group and the barriers to participation were never designed to be removed.

What Genuine Inclusion Would Look Like

  1. Plain-language summaries mandatory for all proposals before voting proceeds
  2. Moderation transparency — all holds/removals publicly logged with stated reasons
  3. Conflict of interest disclosure — service providers must declare financial relationships before commenting on their own proposals
  4. Regional representation in delegate structures — structural commitment, not optics
  5. Community accountability layer — independent of technical teams, focused on process fairness

Closing

The most consequential risk in DAO governance today is not a miscalibrated oracle.

It is the quiet, sustained removal of voices that ask why.

Decentralization without inclusion is not an achievement. It is a rebrand.

@MconnectDAO

governance_posts.title: Should Aave Make Governance Discussions Easier for Non-Technical Users to Follow?
governance_posts.description:
I’ve been reading through several recent Aave governance discussions, especially around V4, risk parameters, new asset onboarding, and the different frameworks used before changes reach an on-chain vote.

One thing I keep noticing is that the quality of the technical discussion is high, but following the full reasoning can be difficult if you are not already familiar with Aave’s governance process, risk terminology, and service-provider structure.

This is not really a criticism of the level of detail. For decisions involving collateral, interest-rate models, caps, liquidations, and protocol risk, that detail is necessary.

What I wonder is whether there is room for an additional layer of communication alongside the technical proposals.

For example, major governance discussions could include a short section explaining the practical user impact in plain language: what changes for suppliers or borrowers, what new risk is being introduced, what problem the proposal is trying to solve, and which assumptions matter most.

That would not replace the technical analysis or reduce the standards required for governance. It could simply make it easier for more Aave users to understand why a proposal matters before deciding whether to follow the discussion more closely.

As Aave V4 introduces new architecture and governance processes continue to evolve, accessibility may become more important simply because there will be more moving parts to understand.

I’m curious how people here think about this. Would a standardized “user impact / plain-language summary” section improve governance participation, or would it add unnecessary duplication to proposals?

governance_posts.description:
Summary

This ARFC proposes to onboard USDe as a supported asset on the Aave V3 X Layer Instance.

Motivation

USDe is Ethena’s synthetic dollar, designed to maintain a value referenced to the US dollar through a combination of protocol held backing assets and offsetting derivatives positions.

USDe has developed significant adoption across DeFi and is currently supported across several Aave markets as both a supplied and borrowed asset.

USDe is deployed on X Layer using Ethena’s LayerZero OFT infrastructure, enabling USDe to move across supported networks through Ethena’s canonical cross-chain deployment.

Onboarding USDe to Aave V3 X Layer would:

  • Expand the range of stablecoin assets available to Aave users on X Layer.
  • Provide an additional asset for lending and borrowing alongside USDT0, USDG, USDC and GHO.
  • Enable USDe to be used as collateral within the general Aave V3 X Layer market.
  • Increase the available stablecoin borrowing liquidity for the existing xBTC, xETH, xSOL, and WOKB E-Mode categories.
  • Expand the range of cross-margin and stablecoin strategies available to users on X Layer.

Enabling USDe as collateral in the general market allows users to access USDe backed borrowing strategies without requiring a dedicated E-Mode configuration.

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.09.22
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase the borrow cap for wstETH from 14,000 to 28,000.
  • Reduce the borrow cap for USDe from 700,000,000 to 100,000,000.

Aave V3 Plasma:

  • Increase the supply cap for USDe from 550,000,000 to 750,000,000.

wstETH (Aave V3 Core)

wstETH sits at 99.8% borrow cap utilization on Aave V3 Core, with 13,977 borrowed against a cap of 14,000.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, September 22, 2026

The top wstETH borrowers have health factors ranging from 1.00 to 4.63, with a median of 1.11 and most of the cohort below 1.16. Their collateral is predominantly weETH by value at $51M (80%), followed by WETH at $8.5M (14%). Given the close correlation among these assets, health factor stability is primarily sensitive to the relative performance of wstETH against the collateral assets, rather than broad market movements.

Recommendation

The proposed cap of 28,000 is approximately 2.00x the current outstanding borrow, resulting in approximately 49.9% post-change cap utilization.

USDe (Aave V3 Plasma)

USDe sits at 100.0% supply cap utilization on Aave V3 Plasma.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, September 22, 2026

The top eight suppliers include six carrying outstanding debt, at health factors between 1.01 and 1.05 with a median of 1.02, and two supplying on a spot basis. All six borrow USDT0 against USDe collateral, and three also hold sUSDe. Since USDe is priced at par with USDT, these positions have very low liquidation risk. Supply is concentrated, with the largest position holding 64.6% of the reserve and the top five holding 94.8%.

Recommendation

The proposed cap of 750,000,000 is approximately 1.36x the current outstanding supply, resulting in approximately 73.3% post-change cap utilization.

Cap Reductions

USDe on Aave V3 Core sits at 11.1% borrow cap utilization (77.9M / 700M). The proposed cap of 100,000,000 is approximately 1.28x current outstanding borrows, landing at approximately 77.9% post-change cap utilization.

Specification

Instance Asset Current Supply Cap Recommended Supply Cap
Aave V3 Plasma USDe 550,000,000 750,000,000
Instance Asset Current Borrow Cap Recommended Borrow Cap
Aave V3 Core wstETH 14,000 28,000
Aave V3 Core USDe 700,000,000 100,000,000

Next Steps

We will move forward and implement these updates via the Risk Steward process. The implemented changes can be reviewed on the LlamaRisk Risk Stewards Dashboard.

This review was independently prepared by LlamaRisk, a DeFi risk service provider funded in part by the Aave DAO. governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Aave Institutional
governance_posts.description:
Summary

Aave Institutional is the DAO’s offchain over-collateralised lending business. It lends dollar stablecoins to institutional borrowers against BTC and ETH held at qualified custodians, at rates materially above what the same dollars earn onchain.

Aave Labs asks the DAO to approve two funding sources for this new business, running in parallel:

  1. A new GHO facilitator with an initial bucket capacity of 25M GHO managed by the GHO Stewards.
  2. The use of DAO balance-sheet assets, pledged as collateral to borrow up to $25M of USDC or USDT.

Loans are advanced primarily in USDC or USDT, so GHO issuance is paced to what GHO can support at the time. The balance sheet carries the first loans so that origination can begin while GHO is grown to support it, and the mix shifts toward GHO over time.

Borrowers pay 6.0% to 8.0% APR against a funding cost of approximately 4.5% on either route. The full net interest margin, 1.50% to 3.50%, accrues to the DAO. Aave Institutional currently holds approximately $300M of deployable borrow demand, and the lead facility is $20M against BTC.

Every funding authorisation requires approval from the GHO Stewards in accordance with current DAO policy (two-of-three multisig between Aave Labs, TokenLogic and LlamaRisk). No GHO is advanced against offchain collateral without the GHO Stewards agreeing to it at the time, on live Stability Module information. Every conversion between GHO and the lending currency is routed and executed jointly with TokenLogic.

Motivation

GHO’s constraint is not mint capacity. It is productive demand that generates yield from outside the protocol at attractive rates. Aave Institutional is that demand.

Aave Institutional opens a market the protocol does not serve today. Institutions want dollar financing against BTC and ETH held with a qualified custodian, on bilaterally negotiated terms, and they will pay above onchain rates for it. It is an established lending market with documented demand, and GHO is well placed to fund it.

Three things make this new business particularly attractive for the DAO:

Attractive Margins: Borrowers pay 6.0% to 8.0% APR, a cost of capital above the rates currently available on Aave Protocol, against a funding cost of approximately 4.5%. The full net interest margin, 1.50% to 3.50%, accrues to the DAO.

Conservative Collateral and Risk Profile: Loans are advanced at a typical 60% to 75% loan-to-value against BTC and ETH. Collateral is held and monitored by a regulated qualified custodian that issues the margin calls and enforces them. Any liquidations are automated via the regulated trading desk of the relevant qualified custodian, rather than sitting with Aave Institutional.

Documented Demand: Aave Institutional currently holds approximately $300M of indicated borrow demand. The lead facility is sized at $20M against BTC at approximately 60% loan-to-value, evergreen with a 90-day notice period on which either party may call the facility or adjust its rate, with tri-party custody and title transfer on default.

Aave already mints GHO against volatile crypto collateral through the V3 facilitator. This proposal applies the same mechanism to collateral of comparable quality at a lower loan-to-value, with a qualified custodian appointed to monitor and enforce it, and at materially better economics for the DAO.

Specification

1. Background

Field Detail
Title Aave Institutional
Mechanism A dedicated facilitator minting GHO against a book of over-collateralised institutional loans secured on BTC and ETH held at qualified custodians
Operator GHO Stewards
Network Ethereum mainnet

2. Lending capacity and funding

GHO funded route:

Field Detail
Capacity 25M GHO under the new facilitator
Use of proceeds Origination of secured institutional loans
GHO Borrow Cap GHO Stewards
Indicative borrower pricing 6.0% to 8.0% APR
Loan tenor 30-day rolling to 12 months
Lending currencies USDC and USDT primarily, GHO where the borrower is amenable
Revenue to the DAO The full net interest margin, 1.50% to 3.50% per annum on the amount drawn

DAO Balance Sheet funded route:

Field Detail
Funding source Over-collateralised borrowing against existing DAO balance-sheet assets on Aave V3 markets
Phase Primary funding source until GHO can support the loans, with facilitator-minted GHO phased in thereafter
Collateral pledged WETH and WBTC, with AAVE capped as set out below
Limit on AAVE as collateral AAVE may not exceed 50% of the collateral pledged to this route, measured at the time of each pledge. Management of subsequent drift in the non-AAVE share sits with the Aave Finance Committee, led by TokenLogic.
Debt asset USDT and USDC, drawn in the currency of the borrower’s facility
Borrowing cost The venue’s prevailing borrow rate, expected 4.0% to 5.0% APR
Size Sufficient collateral to fund up to $25M USD equivalent. This is additional to the facilitator’s 25M GHO bucket capacity, not part of it

3. Peg impact and conversion

Aave Labs considers the effect on the GHO peg the material question on this proposal.

Stability Module redemption inventory across the GHO deployment stood at $59.9M on 24th September 2026, held in two funded instances.

Instance Network Underlying Redeemable
GSM stataUSDT (0x8822…f5e3) Ethereum waEthUSDT 19.2M USDT
GSM stataUSDT0 (0xd061…ebf37) Plasma waPlaUSDT0 40.7M USDT
Total 59.9M USDT

The requested initial capacity of 25M GHO is approximately 42% of current redemption inventory. The USDC instances hold negligible redeemable balance and are excluded. GHO is fungible across networks through Chainlink CCIP, so redemption inventory is a property of the deployment rather than of any single network. DAO service providers are in active conversations with depositors to grow GSM balances and expand capacity under this route.

Minting GHO against offchain collateral carries a legitimate objection. It increases GHO in circulation while placing the backing outside the protocol’s immediate reach, and converting that GHO into stablecoin dollars through the GSM draws on the same inventory that supports the peg.

Two things address this. The first is the authorisation control in Specification 5, which places assessment of Stability Module impact with the GHO Stewards at the point of every funding decision rather than fixing it in advance by a term that could not anticipate market conditions. The second is that loans funded from DAO balance-sheet assets involve no exchange between GHO and the lending currency and draw no Stability Module inventory at all. That is why they carry the initial phase.

Where GHO is the funding source, it is exchanged into the lending currency at drawdown and back into GHO at repayment. Every exchange of GHO is routed and executed jointly with TokenLogic. In practice, this means four things:

  1. The route is agreed before each conversion is executed, in this order of preference: Matched sGHO inflows first, since they are net neutral to the Stability Module by construction and, at matched duration, remain so for the life of the loan. Secondary market liquidity second. The Stability Module last, and only with TokenLogic’s agreement at the time.
  2. Size is tranched and timed rather than executed in a single clip where market depth requires it.
  3. A maximum acceptable deviation from peg is agreed in advance, and a conversion is deferred if it cannot be executed inside that limit.
  4. Every conversion is reported afterwards with size, route, realised price, and any Stability Module inventory used.

Repayment runs the same process in reverse and buys GHO. Across a full loan cycle the directional effect on the peg largely offsets, and the residual cost is execution slippage on each leg rather than a permanent addition to GHO supply.

Aave Institutional also anticipates growing sGHO deposits to support further scaling, and is in discussions with a number of parties to effect this.

4. Mechanism and risk

Every facility is over-collateralised, with collateral value exceeding the loan at origination and maintained above a defined threshold through the life of the loan. Each facility is bilaterally negotiated, so pricing, tenor and loan-to-value are set per counterparty with oversight from the GHO Stewards.

Borrower collateral is held at a leading qualified custodian, which is also appointed as collateral manager for the facility. The custodian monitors collateral value against the agreed thresholds, issues margin calls on a deterioration in collateral price, and liquidates where a call is not met. Each loan is governed by a Master Loan Agreement with legal security interests taken over the collateral, alongside an Account Control Agreement between the lending entity, the borrower and the custodian giving the lender the right to direct the sale of collateral and repay the Aave debt in full on default. Collateral title transfers on default and is not rehypothecated at any point. Monitoring and enforcement therefore sit with a regulated third party rather than with Aave Institutional or the borrower.

Risk Mitigation
Effect on the GHO peg from new supply Every funding authorisation requires GHO Steward approval.
Credit loss on an individual loan Loan-to-value of 60% to 75%, individual underwriting, a defined margin-call cadence, title transfer on default, no rehypothecation, and monitoring and liquidation performed by a qualified custodian rather than by the lender
Slower enforcement than onchain liquidation Loan-to-value is set more conservatively than in the V3 GHO market and tenors are capped at 12 months. Enforcement is executed by the custodian that already holds the collateral, so there is no transfer step between decision and sale
GHO price impact from conversion Every conversion routed, sized and timed jointly with TokenLogic against an agreed maximum deviation from peg, with matched sGHO inflows used first and the Stability Module last. Repayment conversions buy GHO and offset the drawdown leg
Reflexive exposure from AAVE pledged as collateral The conditions in which BTC-backed loans come under stress are the conditions in which AAVE falls, so the collateral weakens at the moment enforcement is tested and a forced sale into a falling market is self-reinforcing. AAVE is capped at 50% of the collateral pledged as part of the balance sheeting funded route, with the balance in WETH and WBTC and position health monitored by TokenLogic
Collateral concentration Scope limited to BTC and ETH. Any extension returns to governance
Custodian Qualified custodians only, with an Account Control Agreement in place with each

5. Governance controls

Control Held by
Bucket capacity, including reduction to zero GHO Stewards, within existing mandate
Facilitator removal Aave DAO
Extension of the collateral set beyond BTC and ETH Aave DAO
Limit on AAVE as balance-sheet collateral Aave Finance Committee
Mint execution GHO Stewards
Expansion of the GHO Borrow Cap GHO Stewards, within existing mandate
Funding authorisation GHO Stewards
Execution of GHO to lending currency conversion Aave Labs jointly with TokenLogic
Collateral management, margin calls and liquidation Qualified custodian appointed for the facility, under the Account Control Agreement
Facilitator contract upgradeability Immutable, with bucket capacity governed by the Aave DAO

6. Facilitator implementation

TokenLogic will deploy a dedicated facilitator contract, registered on the GHO token by governance under FACILITATOR_MANAGER_ROLE, with bucket capacity set under BUCKET_MANAGER_ROLE. Minting is constrained by the standard bucket check, so that bucketLevel plus the minted amount may not exceed bucketCapacity. GHO is minted under GHO Stewards authority, and its use for an eligible institutional loan requires authorisation from them.

Reporting and Offboarding

Aave Labs will publish a regular loan tape to this forum, covering outstanding balance, collateral composition, loan-to-value distribution, margin-call events, realised losses, and the current funding position.

On offboarding, Aave Labs wishes to be explicit about a constraint the DAO should understand before voting rather than discover afterwards. removeFacilitator() requires bucketLevel to be zero, so a lending facilitator creates a position that cannot be fully unwound by governance action alone while loans remain outstanding. Reducing bucket capacity prevents new minting immediately, but it does not retire GHO already issued against live loans.

Three commitments bound that exposure. Term loans written under this facility mature within 12 months maximum. Evergreen facilities carry a call right and a rate-change right in the lender’s favour, typically on 90-day notice, so no loan can outlive a wind-down decision by more than its call period. New origination ceases immediately on a DAO signal, without requiring a vote to compel it.

The worst case is a wind-down over 12 months from the signal, and on the current book it would be materially shorter.

Conclusion

GHO’s constraint is not mint capacity. It is demand that pays for itself, and this is it.

The ask is 25M GHO under a new facilitator, and DAO balance-sheet assets pledged to borrow up to $25M of the lending currency. Together they fund over-collateralised loans to institutional borrowers at 6.0% to 8.0% APR against a funding cost of approximately 4.5% on either route, with the full net interest margin accruing to the DAO.

The yield is external rather than recycled. The collateral is BTC and ETH at 60% to 75% loan-to-value, held at qualified custodians and never rehypothecated. Every loan carries an exit inside 12 months.

Every control that matters stays with the DAO and the GHO Stewards. No draw is funded without the GHO Stewards approving it at the time on live Stability Module information, the first loans draw no Stability Module inventory at all, and AAVE is capped at 50% of the collateral pledged from the balance sheet.

The downside is bounded and governed. The upside is a new, durable external revenue line for GHO and an institutional channel the protocol can scale into.

Next Steps

  1. Gather community ARFC feedback.
  2. If sentiment is favourable, escalate to the Snapshot stage.
  3. Following a positive Snapshot outcome, submit an AIP carrying both authorisations.
    a. Register the facilitator on the GHO token and set initial bucket capacity at 25M GHO.
    b. Authorise the pledging of DAO balance-sheet assets on Aave V3 to borrow up to $25M of USDC/USDT for loan funding, subject to the collateral limits in Specification 2.

Disclaimer

Aave Labs is presenting this proposal in its capacity as a contributor to the Aave ecosystem and is an interested party in its outcome. Aave Institutional is operated by Aave Labs, which would hold one of the three funding authorisation signatures, with the full net interest margin accruing to the Aave DAO. No third parties co-authored this proposal. Pricing, loan-to-value ranges, pipeline size and wind-down timelines are indicative and forward-looking, Stability Module figures are stated as of 24th September 2026, and nothing here constitutes financial, legal or investment advice or an offer to transact.

Every funding authorisation requires approval from the GHO Stewards in accordance with current DAO policy (two-of-three multisig between Aave Labs, TokenLogic and LlamaRisk). No GHO is advanced against offchain collateral without the GHO Stewards agreeing to it at the time, on live Stability Module information. Every conversion between GHO and the lending currency is routed and executed jointly with TokenLogic.

Motivation

GHO’s constraint is not mint capacity. It is productive demand that generates yield from outside the protocol at attractive rates. Aave Institutional is that demand.

Aave Institutional opens a market the protocol does not serve today. Institutions want dollar financing against BTC and ETH held with a qualified custodian, on bilaterally negotiated terms, and they will pay above onchain rates for it. It is an established lending market with documented demand, and GHO is well placed to fund it.

Three things make this new business particularly attractive for the DAO:

Attractive Margins: Borrowers pay 6.0% to 8.0% APR, a cost of capital above the rates currently available on Aave Protocol, against a funding cost of approximately 4.5%. The full net interest margin, 1.50% to 3.50%, accrues to the DAO.

Conservative Collateral and Risk Profile: Loans are advanced at a typical 60% to 75% loan-to-value against BTC and ETH. Collateral is held and monitored by a regulated qualified custodian that issues the margin calls and enforces them. Any liquidations are automated via the regulated trading desk of the relevant qualified custodian, rather than sitting with Aave Institutional.

Documented Demand: Aave Institutional currently holds approximately $300M of indicated borrow demand. The lead facility is sized at $20M against BTC at approximately 60% loan-to-value, evergreen with a 90-day notice period on which either party may call the facility or adjust its rate, with tri-party custody and title transfer on default.

Aave already mints GHO against volatile crypto collateral through the V3 facilitator. This proposal applies the same mechanism to collateral of comparable quality at a lower loan-to-value, with a qualified custodian appointed to monitor and enforce it, and at materially better economics for the DAO.

Specification

1. Background

Field Detail
Title Aave Institutional
Mechanism A dedicated facilitator minting GHO against a book of over-collateralised institutional loans secured on BTC and ETH held at qualified custodians
Operator GHO Stewards
Network Ethereum mainnet

2. Lending capacity and funding

GHO funded route:

Field Detail
Capacity 25M GHO under the new facilitator
Use of proceeds Origination of secured institutional loans
GHO Borrow Cap GHO Stewards
Indicative borrower pricing 6.0% to 8.0% APR
Loan tenor 30-day rolling to 12 months
Lending currencies USDC and USDT primarily, GHO where the borrower is amenable
Revenue to the DAO The full net interest margin, 1.50% to 3.50% per annum on the amount drawn

DAO Balance Sheet funded route:

Field Detail
Funding source Over-collateralised borrowing against existing DAO balance-sheet assets on Aave V3 markets
Phase Primary funding source until GHO can support the loans, with facilitator-minted GHO phased in thereafter
Collateral pledged WETH and WBTC, with AAVE capped as set out below
Limit on AAVE as collateral AAVE may not exceed 50% of the collateral pledged to this route, measured at the time of each pledge. Management of subsequent drift in the non-AAVE share sits with the Aave Finance Committee, led by TokenLogic.
Debt asset USDT and USDC, drawn in the currency of the borrower’s facility
Borrowing cost The venue’s prevailing borrow rate, expected 4.0% to 5.0% APR
Size Sufficient collateral to fund up to $25M USD equivalent. This is additional to the facilitator’s 25M GHO bucket capacity, not part of it

3. Peg impact and conversion

Aave Labs considers the effect on the GHO peg the material question on this proposal.

Stability Module redemption inventory across the GHO deployment stood at $59.9M on 24th September 2026, held in two funded instances.

Instance Network Underlying Redeemable
GSM stataUSDT (0x8822…f5e3) Ethereum waEthUSDT 19.2M USDT
GSM stataUSDT0 (0xd061…ebf37) Plasma waPlaUSDT0 40.7M USDT
Total 59.9M USDT

The requested initial capacity of 25M GHO is approximately 42% of current redemption inventory. The USDC instances hold negligible redeemable balance and are excluded. GHO is fungible across networks through Chainlink CCIP, so redemption inventory is a property of the deployment rather than of any single network. DAO service providers are in active conversations with depositors to grow GSM balances and expand capacity under this route.

Minting GHO against offchain collateral carries a legitimate objection. It increases GHO in circulation while placing the backing outside the protocol’s immediate reach, and converting that GHO into stablecoin dollars through the GSM draws on the same inventory that supports the peg.

Two things address this. The first is the authorisation control in Specification 5, which places assessment of Stability Module impact with the GHO Stewards at the point of every funding decision rather than fixing it in advance by a term that could not anticipate market conditions. The second is that loans funded from DAO balance-sheet assets involve no exchange between GHO and the lending currency and draw no Stability Module inventory at all. That is why they carry the initial phase.

Where GHO is the funding source, it is exchanged into the lending currency at drawdown and back into GHO at repayment. Every exchange of GHO is routed and executed jointly with TokenLogic. In practice, this means four things:

  1. The route is agreed before each conversion is executed, in this order of preference: Matched sGHO inflows first, since they are net neutral to the Stability Module by construction and, at matched duration, remain so for the life of the loan. Secondary market liquidity second. The Stability Module last, and only with TokenLogic’s agreement at the time.
  2. Size is tranched and timed rather than executed in a single clip where market depth requires it.
  3. A maximum acceptable deviation from peg is agreed in advance, and a conversion is deferred if it cannot be executed inside that limit.
  4. Every conversion is reported afterwards with size, route, realised price, and any Stability Module inventory used.

Repayment runs the same process in reverse and buys GHO. Across a full loan cycle the directional effect on the peg largely offsets, and the residual cost is execution slippage on each leg rather than a permanent addition to GHO supply.

Aave Institutional also anticipates growing sGHO deposits to support further scaling, and is in discussions with a number of parties to effect this.

4. Mechanism and risk

Every facility is over-collateralised, with collateral value exceeding the loan at origination and maintained above a defined threshold through the life of the loan. Each facility is bilaterally negotiated, so pricing, tenor and loan-to-value are set per counterparty with oversight from the GHO Stewards.

Borrower collateral is held at a leading qualified custodian, which is also appointed as collateral manager for the facility. The custodian monitors collateral value against the agreed thresholds, issues margin calls on a deterioration in collateral price, and liquidates where a call is not met. Each loan is governed by a Master Loan Agreement with legal security interests taken over the collateral, alongside an Account Control Agreement between the lending entity, the borrower and the custodian giving the lender the right to direct the sale of collateral and repay the Aave debt in full on default. Collateral title transfers on default and is not rehypothecated at any point. Monitoring and enforcement therefore sit with a regulated third party rather than with Aave Institutional or the borrower.

Risk Mitigation
Effect on the GHO peg from new supply Every funding authorisation requires GHO Steward approval.
Credit loss on an individual loan Loan-to-value of 60% to 75%, individual underwriting, a defined margin-call cadence, title transfer on default, no rehypothecation, and monitoring and liquidation performed by a qualified custodian rather than by the lender
Slower enforcement than onchain liquidation Loan-to-value is set more conservatively than in the V3 GHO market and tenors are capped at 12 months. Enforcement is executed by the custodian that already holds the collateral, so there is no transfer step between decision and sale
GHO price impact from conversion Every conversion routed, sized and timed jointly with TokenLogic against an agreed maximum deviation from peg, with matched sGHO inflows used first and the Stability Module last. Repayment conversions buy GHO and offset the drawdown leg
Reflexive exposure from AAVE pledged as collateral The conditions in which BTC-backed loans come under stress are the conditions in which AAVE falls, so the collateral weakens at the moment enforcement is tested and a forced sale into a falling market is self-reinforcing. AAVE is capped at 50% of the collateral pledged as part of the balance sheeting funded route, with the balance in WETH and WBTC and position health monitored by TokenLogic
Collateral concentration Scope limited to BTC and ETH. Any extension returns to governance
Custodian Qualified custodians only, with an Account Control Agreement in place with each

5. Governance controls

Control Held by
Bucket capacity, including reduction to zero GHO Stewards, within existing mandate
Facilitator removal Aave DAO
Extension of the collateral set beyond BTC and ETH Aave DAO
Limit on AAVE as balance-sheet collateral Aave Finance Committee
Mint execution GHO Stewards
Expansion of the GHO Borrow Cap GHO Stewards, within existing mandate
Funding authorisation GHO Stewards
Execution of GHO to lending currency conversion Aave Labs jointly with TokenLogic
Collateral management, margin calls and liquidation Qualified custodian appointed for the facility, under the Account Control Agreement
Facilitator contract upgradeability Immutable, with bucket capacity governed by the Aave DAO

6. Facilitator implementation

TokenLogic will deploy a dedicated facilitator contract, registered on the GHO token by governance under FACILITATOR_MANAGER_ROLE, with bucket capacity set under BUCKET_MANAGER_ROLE. Minting is constrained by the standard bucket check, so that bucketLevel plus the minted amount may not exceed bucketCapacity. GHO is minted under GHO Stewards authority, and its use for an eligible institutional loan requires authorisation from them.

Reporting and Offboarding

Aave Labs will publish a regular loan tape to this forum, covering outstanding balance, collateral composition, loan-to-value distribution, margin-call events, realised losses, and the current funding position.

On offboarding, Aave Labs wishes to be explicit about a constraint the DAO should understand before voting rather than discover afterwards. removeFacilitator() requires bucketLevel to be zero, so a lending facilitator creates a position that cannot be fully unwound by governance action alone while loans remain outstanding. Reducing bucket capacity prevents new minting immediately, but it does not retire GHO already issued against live loans.

Three commitments bound that exposure. Term loans written under this facility mature within 12 months maximum. Evergreen facilities carry a call right and a rate-change right in the lender’s favour, typically on 90-day notice, so no loan can outlive a wind-down decision by more than its call period. New origination ceases immediately on a DAO signal, without requiring a vote to compel it.

The worst case is a wind-down over 12 months from the signal, and on the current book it would be materially shorter.

Conclusion

GHO’s constraint is not mint capacity. It is demand that pays for itself, and this is it.

The ask is 25M GHO under a new facilitator, and DAO balance-sheet assets pledged to borrow up to $25M of the lending currency. Together they fund over-collateralised loans to institutional borrowers at 6.0% to 8.0% APR against a funding cost of approximately 4.5% on either route, with the full net interest margin accruing to the DAO.

The yield is external rather than recycled. The collateral is BTC and ETH at 60% to 75% loan-to-value, held at qualified custodians and never rehypothecated. Every loan carries an exit inside 12 months.

Every control that matters stays with the DAO and the GHO Stewards. No draw is funded without the GHO Stewards approving it at the time on live Stability Module information, the first loans draw no Stability Module inventory at all, and AAVE is capped at 50% of the collateral pledged from the balance sheet.

The downside is bounded and governed. The upside is a new, durable external revenue line for GHO and an institutional channel the protocol can scale into.

Next Steps

  1. Gather community ARFC feedback.
  2. If sentiment is favourable, escalate to the Snapshot stage.
  3. Following a positive Snapshot outcome, submit an AIP carrying both authorisations.
    a. Register the facilitator on the GHO token and set initial bucket capacity at 25M GHO.
    b. Authorise the pledging of DAO balance-sheet assets on Aave V3 to borrow up to $25M of USDC/USDT for loan funding, subject to the collateral limits in Specification 2.

Disclaimer

Aave Labs is presenting this proposal in its capacity as a contributor to the Aave ecosystem and is an interested party in its outcome. Aave Institutional is operated by Aave Labs, which would hold one of the three funding authorisation signatures, with the full net interest margin accruing to the Aave DAO. No third parties co-authored this proposal. Pricing, loan-to-value ranges, pipeline size and wind-down timelines are indicative and forward-looking, Stability Module figures are stated as of 24th September 2026, and nothing here constitutes financial, legal or investment advice or an offer to transact.

governance_posts.title: How Aave Stable Vaults work
governance_posts.description:
Aave Labs open-sourced the Stable Vaults contracts at aave-dao/stable-vault after the July launch. I spent the last week reading the codebase and the architecture docs and wrote up how the system fits together, since there isn’t a single community-level explainer yet.

Corrections welcome a few things below are inferences from the code, and I’ve marked them.

Source: GitHub - aave-dao/stable-vault: Stable, per-user earning rate vault protocol developed by Aave Labs · GitHub and Stable Vault Architecture | Aave Protocol Documentation

1. The problem it solves

Aave market rates are variable. Stable Vaults promise depositors a fixed per-second rate, then earn that yield behind the scenes across Aave markets and other ERC-4626 strategies, on more than one chain. Three design goals show up everywhere in the code:

  1. Principal is always redeemable; interest is only paid out of realized surplus.
  2. Accounting is separated from earning, across chains.
  3. Users never touch a bridge directly.

2. Two kinds of chains

Accounting Chain (Arbitrum for the Aave App deployment). This is the source of truth. It hosts:

  • StableVault - user entry point: deposits, SubVault assignment, the two-step withdrawal.
  • FundsHandler - aggregates the system’s total asset value across local balances and remote chains.
  • Allocator - holds idle funds and moves them into whitelisted ERC-4626 strategies.
  • AccountingChainGateway - sends funds out and validates messages coming back.
  • IouTokenManager, AssetRegistry, PriceOracle, policies.

Earning Chains (one deployment per chain). Each hosts an EarningChainGateway, its own Allocator, and an EarningChainStateProvider that publishes a balance snapshot. Earning chains can only send funds back to their accounting chain, never sideways.

Bridging uses adapters; the repo ships Chainlink CCIP and a.DI adapters.

3. SubVaults and rates

A SubVault is a virtual bucket inside StableVault with its own perSecondRate. Users hold shares in exactly one SubVault; the rate a user earns is whichever SubVault they were assigned to at deposit (via policyData). This is how per-user or per-tier rates work without deploying separate vaults and loyalty tiers, promo rates, and partner-specific rates are just different SubVaults.

4. Deposit flow

deposit(user, asset, amount, policyData) on StableVault:

  1. Asset must be registered in AssetRegistry.
  2. Price is validated through PriceOracle.validatePrice (staleness and min-price checks; prices above 1 RAY are capped to 1 RAY).
  3. Amount is converted to SubVault shares at the current conversion rate; the position is credited.
  4. Funds land idle on the local Allocator. Nothing is deployed to a strategy at deposit time an off-chain manager later calls rebalance().

5. Withdrawal flow (two steps, IOU-based)

Step 1 - requestWithdrawal(user, amountInRay, policyData) on the accounting chain. Shares are burned and the user receives IOU tokens denominated in the common unit (USD). The principal portion of a position is always claimable as IOUs; the interest portion is gated by the system’s trusted surplus.

Step 2 - executeWithdrawal(...) on the accounting chain, or exchangeIouTokens(...) on an earning chain. IOUs are burned, the WithdrawalExecutionPolicy applies fees/operational costs, assets are pulled from the local Allocator, and the user receives their chosen output asset.

IOUs can be bridged between chains via IouTokenManager.bridgeTokens. The stated reason is liveness: users can exit on an earning chain even if managers are offline and haven’t repatriated funds. Note the bridge fee is paid by the caller and pulled by the specific bridge adapter, the README explicitly warns to approve only the quoted fee, not unlimited allowance.

6. Multi-asset and the 1:1 swap rule

The vault accepts several stablecoins interchangeably (deposit USDC, withdraw USDT). Swaps inside the Allocator go through a Swapper and are enforced at a nominal 1:1 rate. Any slippage or venue fee is covered by an external Slippage Coverage Vault, not by depositors.

7. Surplus and the cross-chain oracle

This is the part I found most interesting. FundsHandler computes total system value by summing local balances plus each registered earning chain’s balance, read on demand from ChainBalanceOracle. Earning-chain balances come from EarningChainStateProvider.getState() snapshots published through a Chainlink bundle feed and decoded by ChainlinkChainBalanceOracleAdapter.

If a snapshot is stale (heartbeat + buffer exceeded), that chain contributes zero to the total. So a lagging oracle makes the system under-estimate surplus, which delays interest withdrawals rather than overpaying them. Inbound RETURN_FUNDS / BURN_IOU_TOKEN messages are also validated against the source-chain block number in the latest snapshot.

8. Manager roles (the off-chain half)

Managers can:

  • pushFundsToChain (accounting → earning) and pushFundsToAccountingChain (back).
  • Add / remove / trust / distrust / order strategies on each Allocator.
  • Call rebalance() to move funds between strategies or swap assets.

Inference: the repo contains contracts plus deploy scripts only. The service that decides when to rebalance and how much to send to each chain and strategy — effectively an allocation solver under constraints (promised SubVault rates, pending IOU liquidity, bridge cost, strategy trust ordering) — is not in the public repo. If anyone from Aave Labs can say whether that layer is planned to be opened, I’d be interested.

9. Security

The audits/ folder has ten reports from Certora, ChainSecurity and J. Feist dated Jan–Jul 2026, including a separate Certora review of the a.DI adapter. License is proprietary (All Rights Reserved under Aave Labs), so this is source-available rather than open-source. Bug bounty details are listed as “coming soon”.

10. Diagram

Open questions

  1. Which chains are live as earning chains today, and what’s the current strategy list per Allocator?
  2. How is the SubVault rate chosen relative to realized strategy yield — is there a target coverage ratio (surplus / promised interest) that triggers rate changes?
  3. Is the manager/rebalancer expected to be permissioned indefinitely, or is there a path to a Risk Steward-style bounded automation like the DAO uses for v3 parameters?
  4. Any plans to publish a subgraph or indexer schema for StableVault / IouTokenManager events? I’m building an open one and would rather align with something official.

Happy to be corrected on any of the above and I’ve tried to stick to what’s in the code.

Kumar Shivam - Github & X

governance_posts.title: [Direct-To-AIP] Onboard PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 to Aave V3 Monad Instance
governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-To-AIP] Onboard PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 to Aave V3 Monad Instance

author: @TokenLogic

created: 2026-09-25

Summary

This proposal lists PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 on Aave V3 Monad ahead of the existing PT-AUSD maturity on 8 October 2026. The December PT would launch with the same risk parameters used for the October listing, with borrowing disabled and collateral use limited to a dedicated stablecoin eMode.

Motivation

PT-AUSD-8OCT2026 matures on 8 October 2026. Pendle has deployed the next AUSD market with a maturity of 17 December 2026, and this listing would allow users to roll into the December PT and continue using their positions as collateral on Aave V3 Monad.

The October PT was listed through AIP 513, following the ARFC and a Snapshot vote with 99.99% support. As of 25 September 2026, approximately 63.9M PT-AUSD-8OCT2026 is supplied against an 80M supply cap.

The December PT uses the same underlying asset, Pendle market factory and pricing approach. This proposal follows the Direct-to-AIP process for the next maturity, using the October listing’s launch parameters, including an initial supply cap of 20M.

Specification

Field Value
Asset PT-AUSD-17DEC2026
PT token 0x8B562578b2f9Aa8C14cCda3c5d6CBCEaD3B06a57
Pendle market 0x9cbc42eff240ad2e43bbdc3c0562a9b4ce842a5a
SY token 0xE99f124109752f8e62B4fd5c7E3C01C1BBF58B24
YT token 0x211EDf350b927C6EAE808a63D5f6318Bac5A7e5e
Underlying (AUSD) 0x00000000eFE302BEAA2b3e6e1b18d08D69a9012a
Decimals 6
Maturity 17 December 2026

eMode

A dedicated eMode will allow users to supply PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 as collateral and borrow USDT0, USDC, GHO or USDe. Its parameters and borrowable assets match the PT_Agora__Stablecoins eMode created for the October PT.

eMode ID eMode Collateral Borrowable LTV LT Liq. Bonus Isolated
6 PT_AUSD_17DEC2026__Stablecoins PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 USDT0, USDC, GHO, USDe 93% 95% 2.44% Yes
