governance_posts.title: AL Development Update | September 2026
governance_posts.description:
Greetings, Aave community!

Aave Labs has continued to make steady progress across multiple protocol initiatives in line with its service provider scope.

During September, Aave V4 expanded to two new networks and surpassed $1B in deposits, while work advanced across risk management, integrations, technical assessments, governance, and product development. The update below reflects Aave Labs’ transparent and collaborative approach to building in public.

September update:

  • Released the official Aave Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, enabling AI tools and agents to interact with Aave.
  • Aave V4 surpassed $1B in deposits, reaching a new record high.
  • Activated Aave V4 on Arc and on Base, where the Equities Hub enables Coinbase tokenized equities to be used as collateral.
  • Activated the Aave V4 Risk Stewards on Ethereum, Avalanche, and Base for routine risk parameter adjustments, with a tailored configuration for the tokenized equities on Base.
  • Onboarded PAXG to the Aave V4 Global Dollar Hub.
  • Published the Custodied Collateral Lending ARFC.
  • Continued working with the Babylon team on the integration and its launch.
  • Executed the Low Adoption Asset Deprecation and advanced the oracle deprecation across Aave V2 and V3.
  • Conducted and published the technical assessments of Arc and its launch reserves, USDC on X Layer, and the Coinbase tokenized equities on Base.
  • Expanded early access to the Aave App and enabled USDC and USDT on Ethereum.
  • Added Base support to Aave Pro, delivered a new look for the Aave V3 interface, and launched a token relations dashboard.
  • Continued development across GHO and Aave Horizon.

Aave Protocol

The team released the official Aave MCP server, which lets AI tools and agents interact with Aave through any MCP client, without authentication, an API key, or signup.

Aave V4

Aave V4 continued its growth during September. Deposits surpassed $1B for the first time alongside $310M in active loans. Deposits on the Avalanche deployment grew from approximately $20M to $30M, while USDG neared $100M on Aave V4.

Aave V4 also expanded to two new networks. The protocol went live on Arc (Snapshot) with USDC, EURC, cirBTC, and WETH available as reserves from launch. @LlamaRisk provided the risk analysis and Chainlink the price feeds. Further proposals will be raised to activate cross-chain governance on the network. The deployment on Base (Snapshot) followed, with the Equities Hub as its first market. The Hub lists seven Coinbase tokenized equities as collateral, with USDC as the only borrowable asset. Both activations were carried out by the Aave V4 Protocol Security Council, as part of the hardening process for the new deployments.

Risk management on Aave V4 reached an important milestone, as the Aave V4 Risk Stewards (Snapshot) were activated on Ethereum, Avalanche, and Base through AIP 523. The Risk Stewards can now apply routine risk parameter adjustments within bounds set by governance, bringing the model established on Aave V3 to Aave V4 and reducing the need for frequent intervention by the Aave V4 Protocol Security Council. As activity increased, rounds 15, 16, and 17 of Add Cap and Draw Cap adjustments were implemented through the Aave V4 Protocol Security Council, while round 18 was executed through the Risk Stewards. Going forward, parameter updates will follow the standard Risk Steward process and its usual communications, rather than regular updates on the Aave V4 Ethereum forum thread.

Integration work also advanced. PAXG from Paxos went live on the Global Dollar Hub through AIP 516. The proposal deployed the PAXG Gold Spoke, where users can borrow USDG against PAXG, and made USDG borrowable on the Pendle Spoke.

We also published the Custodied Collateral Lending ARFC, which proposes a new Aave V4 Isolated Hub and Spoke where institutions could borrow stablecoins against collateral held with a qualified custodian. In parallel, we continued working together with the Babylon team to review and harden the integration’s implementation, and to coordinate its launch.

Aave V3

Aave V3 activity remained robust during September. Active loans reached $12.5B, weETH crossed $4B in deposits, and the X Layer deployment neared $200M in deposits.

The Low Adoption Asset Deprecation proposed by @LlamaRisk was executed through AIP 521, which the team implemented. It winds down reserves with limited adoption, reducing the protocol’s risk surface. In parallel, the team advanced the implementation of @LlamaRisk’s Oracle Deprecation across Aave V2 and V3, and the corresponding AIP is in preparation.

@LlamaRisk’s LlamaGuard PT risk oracle went live on Aave, following the team’s review of its implementation in August. It runs on the Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) and dynamically manages PT collateral risk. The configuration change applied to the Aave V3 Risk Steward in August was also carried over to the Aave V4 Risk Stewards through AIP 523.

Governance Proposals

Governance work during September combined proposals prepared by Aave Labs with technical review for other DAO Service Providers.

We created 4 AIPs:

  • AIP 516: Onboard PAXG to Aave V4 Global Dollar Hub.
  • AIP 520: Maintenance: Grant AL RETRY_ROLE on a.DI (Part 2).
  • AIP 521: Low Adoption Asset Deprecation on Aave V3.
  • AIP 523: Aave V4 Risk Stewards Activation.

The team also reviewed 4 AIPs created by DAO Service Providers:

  • AIP 517: Add X Layer Loop Tool & Margin Trading to FlashBorrowers.
  • AIP 518: USDC GSM Arbitrum.
  • AIP 519: Onboard USDC to Aave V3 X Layer.
  • AIP 522: Safety Module August 2026 - Allowance Update.

Technical Assessments

Technical assessment work supported the month’s network expansion and listings. We published the network assessment of Arc ahead of the Aave V4 deployment on the network, together with asset assessments of USDC, EURC, cirBTC, and WETH, the reserves available at launch. The team also published the assessment of USDC on X Layer.

What else are we working on?

GHO

The Aave Savings Rate was increased to 4.50% APR, available to users depositing into Savings GHO. The team also reviewed AIP 518, through which @TokenLogic deployed the USDC GHO Stability Module (GSM) on Arbitrum, as well as the September GHO Stewards update, which raised the GHO borrow rate on Horizon and adjusted the GSM burn fees.

Aave App

Early access to the Aave App expanded throughout September, with Ghost Pass drops shared across X, Instagram, and Telegram, including drops dedicated to users in the United States. Ghost Pass claiming was also added through skate.aave.com, and all Ghost Passes offered to the Base community were claimed. USDC deposits from Base went live in the app, and USDC and USDT were enabled on Ethereum.

Aave Horizon

Two new assets advanced under the Horizon asset onboarding process: HINC, the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund, and mWIN, a tokenized fixed income portfolio managed by Wellington Management and issued by Midas. Both ARFCs progressed through community discussion, and @LlamaRisk published its support for onboarding HINC. The team’s technical assessments of both assets are in progress.

Aave Pro

Aave Pro supported Aave V4 on Arc from launch, with the new market available on pro.aave.com. Support for Base also shipped, including trading of tokenized equities. The app now displays the underlying yield for supported tokens and uses readable URLs in place of base64 hashes, for example pro.aave.com/explore/token/USDC. More selections now persist across the app, so filters retain previous choices when returning to a page, and performance improvements made the interface faster and more reliable. Work continued on the new Earn and Borrow flows, light mode, and leverage and position swaps.

Aave Interface

The Aave V3 interface was redesigned during September, refreshing the experience across the app and introducing dark mode. Asset swaps and position swaps, powered by CoW Swap, also went live on the Plasma market, allowing users to swap assets, as well as collateral and debt positions.

Aave Web

A new token relations dashboard went live, presenting key statistics on the Aave Protocol, with further metrics planned for its next version.

What’s coming next?

Our main focus for the coming month will be:

  • Raise the proposals to activate cross-chain governance for Aave V4 on Arc.
  • Continue coordinating the Babylon integration launch with the Babylon team.
  • Create the AIP for the oracle deprecation across Aave V2 and V3.
  • Complete the technical assessments of HINC and mWIN for Aave Horizon.
  • Introduce the new Earn and Borrow flows in Aave Pro.
  • Add light mode to Aave Pro.
  • Add leverage and position swaps to Aave Pro.
  • Expand the token relations dashboard with further metrics.

Stay tuned for next month’s update.

Aave Labs

governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 X Layer:

  • Decrease Slope 2 for USDC from 40.00% to 20.00%.

Aave V3 Gnosis:

  • Reduce supply cap for sDAI from 20M to 5M.
  • Reduce supply cap for WXDAI from 4M to 1M.
  • Reduce borrow cap for WXDAI from 3.7M to 500K.

USDC Interest Rate Model (Aave V3 X Layer)

The recommendation lowers Slope 2 on USDC from 40.00% to 20.00%, matching the USD₮0 curve on the same instance. The optimal utilization point (90.00%), base rate (0.00%), and Slope 1 (4.50%) are unchanged. At the current 89.4% utilization, below the optimal point, the variable borrow rate remains 4.47% APR and the supply rate 3.60% APR.

The change applies only above the optimal point, where it halves the rate increase per point of utilization.

Withdrawal Liquidity

Instance Asset Supplied Borrowed Utilization Idle Liquidity
Aave V3 X Layer USDC 6.72M 6.01M 89.4% 712K

The optimal utilization is unchanged, so borrow capacity before Slope 2 engages, and the withdrawal buffer at the optimal point (approximately 672K at current supply) is unaffected. Above the optimal point, the lower Slope 2 moderates the rate response to further supply withdrawals, and utilization warrants monitoring while supply continues to decline.

Cap Reductions

The following reductions are proposed due to low secondary-market liquidity for these assets on Gnosis.

  • sDAI on Aave V3 Gnosis sits at 23.1% supply cap utilization. The proposed cap of 5M is approximately 1.08x the current outstanding supply, resulting in approximately 92.5% post-change cap utilization.
  • WXDAI on Aave V3 Gnosis sits at 19.9% supply cap utilization. The proposed cap of 1M is approximately 1.26x the current outstanding supply, resulting in approximately 79.5% post-change cap utilization. The borrow cap moves to 500K, approximately 1.08x the current outstanding borrows, resulting in approximately 92.3% post-change borrow cap utilization.

IRM

governance_posts.title: [ARFC] The Aave Foundation, Phase 1
governance_posts.description:
Summary

This ARFC seeks to establish the Aave Foundation, a memberless Cayman Islands foundation company created to hold title to the Aave trademark and related intellectual property for the benefit of the Aave Protocol.

Formation is the first of several phases. This proposal covers Phase 1 only, which provides for the incorporation of the entity and the appointment of its initial independent director and supervisor. Later phases, covering transfer of the trademark, domains, and codebase IP, and operational scope, will each return to governance with their own scope.

This proposal stems from the Aave Will Win Framework commitment to bringing a community-protected vehicle for the brand and IP to governance, reinforcing AAVE as the single asset at the center of the Aave ecosystem.

Phase 1 requests funding only for the reasonable costs of incorporation, legal work, and the appointment of the director, supervisor and secretary. Everything else in this document is structure, scope, and the limits placed on that structure.

Motivation

Aave governance has funded various service providers for years, producing code, risk tooling, models, and documentation. Ownership of that output has been handled inconsistently across engagements, and in several cases it sits with whichever provider happened to build it. The Aave trademark and the primary domains sit outside DAO control today as well. A DAO cannot register a trademark, cannot bring an infringement action, and cannot hold title to a domain, so the practical result is that the DAO has paid for assets it cannot defend.

A Cayman foundation company solves that problem since it can hold title, execute contracts, and appear in court, while remaining memberless so that no member holds rights over it. DeFi foundations have drawn scrutiny for accumulating discretion over time, usually because they were funded by annual treasury grants and staffed by the same team that proposed them. The design proposed below removes both of those conditions.

Forming the entity, transferring registered marks across jurisdictions, and negotiating assignment terms into existing agreements each carry their own legal work and their own costs. A phased approach keeps each request well defined, scoped to work the community can evaluate, and reviewable before the next phase begins. The DAO can stop after any phase and the Foundation will remain a functioning entity with defined governance.

Specification

1. Legal structure

The Aave Foundation is incorporated in the Cayman Islands under the Foundation Companies Act as a memberless foundation company whose objects, as stated in its memorandum of association, are limited to holding, protecting and licensing intellectual property for the benefit of the Aave Protocol. The Foundation is managed by an independent director and supervised by an independent supervisor unaffiliated with the director. After the initial appointments, directors are appointed and removed only by AIP.

Neither Aave Labs, nor any service provider engaged by the DAO, nor any of their affiliates, holds any right to appoint a director or supervisor, or may be appointed to either role.

2. What the Foundation holds

The Foundation will take legal title to the Aave trademark, the protocol codebase IP transferred to it, the primary domains, and the intellectual property assigned to it under service provider agreements. As owner, it is responsible for prosecution, maintenance, and defense and enforcement of those assets.

Brand licensing is unidirectional. The Foundation licenses the Aave name back for product work so that Aave-branded products can keep shipping, and it charges nothing for that license.

The DAO continues to select service providers, set their scope, and approve their compensation through existing governance. Assignment of the resulting code, tooling, models, and documentation to the Foundation becomes a standard condition of those engagements, which gives the DAO one durable owner for accumulated technical work and leaves the Foundation no say over what gets built or who builds it.

3. Funding

The DAO covers reasonable costs for incorporation, qualified secretary onboarding, legal fees, and the trademark and IP transfer mechanics.

No recurring budget is requested, and any future funding needs requires their own governance proposal.

4. Authority of the DAO

Every listing, parameter change, budget, provider engagement, and framework amendment remains a DAO decision made through existing governance.

By AIP, the DAO may appoint and remove directors; holds a consent right over any amendment to the Foundation’s constitution, any disposal of its core IP, and any merger or restructuring; and may direct the Foundation’s winding-up and the transfer of its remaining assets to a successor.

5. Reporting

The Foundation publishes a quarterly report to the governance forum covering assets held and any change in title, operating expenses, and any legal action taken to defend the trademark or codebase. The first report is published within 90 days of the end of the first full calendar quarter of operation.

What to Expect

The Foundation serves a very explicit purpose as outlined above, while governance maintains every decision about the protocol, exactly as it does today. Listings, parameters, budgets, provider selection, and framework amendments stay with tokenholders, and the Foundation has no vote, veto, or advisory role in any of them.

The Foundation has no members or shareholders, and no person holds ownership rights over it. Its board is an independent director, its supervisor is an independent provider unaffiliated with that director, and neither Aave Labs nor any DAO service provider holds a seat or an appointment right.

Each phase of its development returns to the forum as a separate proposal with a separate vote, and the community can decline any of them.

Next steps

If community consensus is reached on this ARFC, the proposal moves to Snapshot, followed by an AIP authorizing reasonable incorporation, legal, and director appointment fees. Incorporation in the Cayman Islands follows, along with appointment of the independent director and the supervisor.

Transfer of the trademark, the domains, and the codebase IP begins once the entity exists and can hold title. Assignment terms enter new service provider engagements as those engagements come up for renewal or replacement through normal governance.

FAQ

Does this give Aave Labs control over the protocol?

No, the protocol is governed by the DAO via tokenholders. Additionally, Aave Labs holds no board seat, no supervisor role, and no appointment rights for the Foundation. The Foundation is memberless, so no shareholder sits above the Aave ecosystem in its statute, and the same restrictions apply to every service provider the DAO engages.

What changes about governance?

Nothing. Listings, parameters, budgets, provider engagements, and framework amendments all remain DAO decisions through the existing process. The Foundation holds title to assets and has no discretion over protocol decisions.

Why the Cayman Islands?

A foundation company under the Cayman Foundation Companies Act can exist without members or shareholders while still holding legal title, executing contracts, and appearing in court. That is what makes it possible to own the trademark and defend it without creating an owner who sits above the DAO.

What happens if the DAO wants to unwind the Foundation?

The DAO may, by AIP, replace the directors at any time, or direct the winding-up of the Foundation, and determine the application of its remaining assets, including their transfer to a successor vehicle, subject in each case to the directors’ fiduciary and statutory duties and applicable law.

What IP transfers, and when?

The Aave trademark, the primary domains, and the protocol codebase IP transfer once the entity exists. Intellectual property produced under future service provider engagements is assigned as a standard condition of those agreements.

Disclaimer

This proposal was authored by Aave Labs. Aave Labs holds no governance or economic role in the Foundation described above and does not receive any portion of the setup grant.

governance_posts.title: [GHO Stewards] October 2026 - GHO Borrow Rate Update
governance_posts.description:
title: [GHO Stewards] October 2026 - GHO Borrow Rate Update
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-10-02

Summary

We propose increasing the GHO borrow rate on Aave V3 Ethereum Core from 4.25% to 4.50% APR and the GHO base rate on Ethereum Prime from 2.75% to 3.00%.

The Core rate will match the Aave Savings Rate, while Prime will retain the 25 bps discount to Core at optimal utilization established in August. The GHO Risk Council will execute both changes under the GHO Stewards mandate.

Motivation

Overview

In August, the Core GHO borrow rate increased to 4.25% in two steps, and the Aave Savings Rate was set at 4.50%. A further increase in the Core rate was intended to follow once USDC and USDT borrowing costs reached 4.50%. Both now stand at 4.39%, close to that level, while GHO remains cheaper to borrow at 4.25%.

Borrowers currently pay 4.25% to mint GHO on Core and can earn 4.50% by depositing it into sGHO. The DAO funds this 25 bps difference. At 4.50%, the Core borrow rate would match the savings rate and sit slightly above current USDC and USDT borrowing costs.

Prime

The Prime adjustment follows the same approach agreed in August: the GHO borrow rate at optimal utilization remains 25 bps below Core. With a base rate of 3.00%, Prime’s rate at the kink would rise from 4.00% to 4.25%. At the 86% utilization recorded in this update, borrowers would pay approximately 4.17%, up from 3.92%. The rest of the interest rate curve is unchanged.

Peg and the GHO Stability Modules

GHO traded below $0.999 for most of September and closed 1 October near $0.9993. Over the same period, GSM redemption reserves declined. The USDC GSM is now depleted, while the USDT GSM holds approximately 22.5M USDT.

Some borrowers may repay GHO debt following the rate increase. Those who need to acquire GHO can buy it on the secondary market or mint it through a GSM using USDC or USDT, with no mint fee. Secondary-market purchases would support the peg; minting through the GSMs would replenish their stablecoin reserves. If GHO returns to par, GSM minting should become more attractive relative to market purchases.

We expect continued sGHO deposits through the Aave App to offset part of any decline in borrowed GHO.

Aave Institutional

The [ARFC] Aave Institutional proposal identifies matched sGHO inflows, secondary market liquidity and GSM redemption reserves as funding sources for its GHO route. As we noted in the discussion, current GSM reserves do not cover the full facilitator capacity, and the initial loans will be funded from the DAO balance sheet. As lending grows, the route will need more USDC available through the GSMs. This rate adjustment should help replenish those reserves if borrowers repay using GHO minted through the modules.

Specification

Both rates will increase by 25 bps in a single update per instance, within the GhoAaveSteward per-update limit.
The GHO Risk Council will execute the changes through updateGhoBorrowRate on the Core and Prime GhoAaveSteward contracts. After execution, we will monitor GHO’s peg, GSM reserves, sGHO deposits and GHO debt on both instances.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

governance_posts.title: [Discussion] A second, issuer-controlled verifier for cross-chain GHO on CCIP 2.0
governance_posts.description:
Hi everyone,

Cross-chain GHO runs on Chainlink CCIP: GHO is locked on Ethereum and minted through facilitators on other chains. CCIP 2.0, live since September 28, now lets a token pool require additional verifiers on top of Chainlink’s committee.

We built Countersign. Countersign is an issuer-operated Cross-Chain Verifier (CCV) for Chainlink CCIP 2.0 that runs as a CRE workflow, so there are no servers to operate. The token pool refuses to mint or release a large transfer until Countersign has independently re-checked it: the canonical OnRamp event, the cross-chain supply invariant (and Proof of Reserve when available), rolling outflow and per-sender limits, and a denylist. A guardian can hold a suspicious transfer for review, and a tighten-only circuit breaker freezes lanes if supply ever looks unbacked.

For GHO it can enforce the core invariant directly: GHO minted on remote chains never exceeds GHO locked on Ethereum, checked for every transfer before the mint, plus rolling outflow limits per lane.

Live on public testnets, including a transfer held and then released by a guardian:

  • 2-minute demo: https://youtu.be/FKoKNaHxgg0
  • Open-source code, 99 tests and every testnet transaction: GitHub - allertrack/countersign: countersign · GitHub

We’d welcome feedback from the community and service providers on whether a testnet pilot on GHO’s lanes is worthwhile, and which thresholds and limits would make sense. Countersign only adds checks: it cannot move funds or loosen rate limits.

Pablo, Countersign

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.10.07
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase supply cap for PT-srUSDe-22OCT2026 from 10,000,000 to 20,000,000.

Aave V3 Polygon:

  • Increase supply cap for WETH from 15,000 to 20,000.

Aave V3 Mantle:

  • Increase supply cap for USDe from 40,000,000 to 80,000,000.
  • Reduce borrow cap for USDe from 18,000,000 to 10,000,000.

Aave V3 Base:

  • Increase supply cap for cbBTC from 3,200 to 4,000.
  • Increase supply cap for cbETH from 50,000 to 60,000.

PT-srUSDe-22OCT2026 (Aave V3 Core)

PT-srUSDe-22OCT2026 has reached 92.1% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

The top suppliers have health factors ranging from 1.02 to 73.98, with a median of 1.07. USDC is the dominant borrowed asset by a wide margin, followed by USDT and USDe, all held against PT collateral within the PT-srUSDe E-Mode categories, so the health factor of the cohort is driven primarily by the PT’s discount to par.

Liquidity


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

The primary trading venue is the Pendle AMM pool on Ethereum, which holds 3.89M in total liquidity, split 53% PT and 47% SY. Pool TVL has eased from approximately 4.6M in early August, while the implied APY has risen from around 4% to between 5.5% and 6% over the same period. The PT matures on October 22, 2026, after which it becomes redeemable at par against the underlying, so the exit at maturity does not depend on secondary market depth.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 10M to 20M on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 46.1% post-change cap utilization.

WETH (Aave V3 Polygon)

WETH is currently at 89.2% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Polygon instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

The top suppliers run health factors between 1.55 and 13.04, with a median of 2.26, and 19 of 20 carry outstanding debt. Debt is denominated predominantly in stablecoins, with USDC the most widely borrowed, followed by USDT0, and WBTC is the most common additional collateral, so the health factor of the cohort tracks the ETH price.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 15,000 to 20,000 on Aave V3 Polygon, which places the reserve at approximately 66.9% post-change cap utilization. The borrow cap is unchanged.

USDe (Aave V3 Mantle)

USDe is currently at 86.0% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Mantle instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

Supply is concentrated in a small number of positions, which run health factors between 1.00 and 1.07 with a median of 1.02, and 7 of 9 carry outstanding debt. Debt is denominated almost entirely in USDT0 and is held against USDe and sUSDe collateral within the stablecoin E-Mode categories. USDe is priced through the USDT/USD feed, the same feed that prices the USDT0 debt, so the liquidation risk is low and dependent on the incentive and borrow rate spread.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 40M to 80M on Aave V3 Mantle, which places the reserve at approximately 43.0% post-change cap utilization. Outstanding USDe borrowing stands at 2,433 against the 18M borrow cap, and we recommend reducing the borrow cap to 10M, which remains well above current borrowing.

cbBTC (Aave V3 Base)

cbBTC has reached 90.6% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Base instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

Supply is broadly distributed, and the top suppliers run health factors between 1.24 and 3.43, with a median of 2.10, with all 20 carrying outstanding debt. USDC is the dominant borrowed asset, with WETH debt in a minority of positions, so the health factor of the cohort tracks the BTC price.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 3,200 to 4,000 on Aave V3 Base, which places the reserve at approximately 72.5% post-change cap utilization. The borrow cap is unchanged.

cbETH (Aave V3 Base)

cbETH has reached 96.8% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Base instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 7, 2026

Supply is concentrated in a small number of positions, which run health factors between 1.02 and 17.23 with a median of 1.27, and all 20 carry outstanding debt. WETH is the dominant borrowed asset by a wide margin, with USDC second, and the largest positions hold cbETH against WETH within the ETH-correlated E-Mode categories, so their health factors depend on the cbETH to ETH exchange rate.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 50,000 to 60,000 on Aave V3 Base, which places the reserve at approximately 80.7% post-change cap utilization.

Specification

Supply Caps

Aave V3 Polygon WETH 15,000 20,000
Aave V3 Mantle USDe 40,000,000 80,000,000
Aave V3 Base cbBTC 3,200 4,000
Aave V3 Base cbETH 50,000 60,000

Borrow Caps

Instance Asset Current Borrow Cap Recommended Borrow Cap
Aave V3 Mantle USDe 18,000,000 10,000,000

Next Steps

governance_posts.title: [Direct-to-AIP] Asset Listing - USDG Arbitrum
governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-to-AIP] Asset Listing - USDG Arbitrum
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-10-08

Summary

This publication proposes to onboard USDG as a supported asset on the Aave V3 Arbitrum Instance.

USDG would join the instance as a borrowable stablecoin, giving Arbitrum users another option to supply and borrow.

Motivation

USDG is a stablecoin issued by Paxos. According to Paxos documentation, USDG on Arbitrum is deployed through LayerZero OFT from Ethereum.

USDG is listed on Aave V3 Ethereum Core, Aave V3 X Layer, Aave V3 Ink (Tydro), and Aave V4 Ethereum through the Core Hub and the Global Dollar Hub, with collateral use disabled in each market. USDG supply on Aave is growing quickly, rising from $94.1M to $123.2M over the last 90 days, which makes USDG a strong candidate stablecoin for the Aave V3 Arbitrum Instance.

On Aave V3 Arbitrum, stablecoin liquidity is concentrated in the USDC and USD₮0 reserves, both of which run at high utilisation, while the other stablecoin reserves on the instance are frozen or small.

Onboarding USDG to Aave V3 Arbitrum would:

  • Provide an additional borrowable stablecoin alongside USDC and USD₮0.
  • Add borrowing capacity without increasing the instance’s collateral risk, as USDG would not be active as collateral.
  • Extend USDG’s presence on Aave to Arbitrum, in line with its listings on other Aave markets.

The listing would bring a Paxos-issued stablecoin to Arbitrum and give USDG holders on the network a market to supply into.

Specification

USDG Contract Address

The address above represents Paxos’s USDG deployment on Arbitrum.

Proposed Market Configuration

We propose initially configuring USDG with the following parameters, subject to final recommendations from Aave Risk Service Providers.

Parameter Value
Asset USDG
Isolation Mode No
Borrowable Yes
Collateral Enabled No
Supply Cap 30,000,000
Borrow Cap 27,600,000
Debt Ceiling -
LTV 0.00%
LT 0.00%
Liquidation Bonus 0.00%
Liquidation Protocol Fee 10%
Variable Base 0.00%
Variable Slope 1 4.00%
Variable Slope 2 30.00%
Uoptimal 90.00%
Reserve Factor 10%
Stable Borrowing Disabled
Flashloanable Yes
Siloed Borrowing No
Borrowable in Isolation Yes
eModes -

The proposed configuration excludes USDG from collateral use, consistent with its listings on the other Aave instances. It uses the same interest rate curve as the USDC reserve on Aave V3 Arbitrum and sets a 10% reserve factor, matching USDC and USD₮0 on Arbitrum and USDG on X Layer and Ink.

We consider USDG’s secondary-market liquidity on Arbitrum, concentrated in the Fluid USDG/USDC pool, sufficient for an initial listing.

Final onboarding parameters remain subject to review and recommendations from Aave’s Risk Service Providers.

Oracle

A Chainlink USDG/USD Price Feed is available on Arbitrum.

Consistent with the oracle configuration USDG uses on Aave V3 Ethereum Core, Ink, and X Layer, we propose pricing USDG with the Chainlink USDG/USD feed, along with a Capped USDG/USD adapter at a 1.04 price cap.

The final oracle contract, adapter deployment, and configuration remain subject to confirmation by the relevant Aave Risk and Technical Service Providers.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the community.
  2. Using the Direct-to-AIP process, incorporate feedback from the Risk Service Provider and the Technical Service Provider.
  3. Deposit at least $150 worth of USDG into the Aave Short Executor before the market goes live, as required by Aave Governance Framework v2.
  4. Escalate this proposal to the AIP Voting stage.

Copyright

Copyright and related rights waived via CC0.

  • Add borrowing capacity without increasing the instance’s collateral risk, as USDG would not be active as collateral.
  • Extend USDG’s presence on Aave to Arbitrum, in line with its listings on other Aave markets.

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.10.08
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Monad:

  • Increase supply cap for USDe from 100,000,000 to 150,000,000.
  • Increase supply cap for AUSD from 20,000,000 to 40,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for AUSD from 18,000,000 to 32,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for mUSD from 25,000,000 to 40,000,000.
  • Reduce supply cap for PT-AUSD-8OCT2026 from 80,000,000 to 1.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Reduce supply cap for USDe from 700,000,000 to 550,000,000.

USDe (Aave V3 Monad)

USDe is currently at 89.8% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 8, 2026

Supply is concentrated in a small number of positions, which run health factors between 1.01 and 1.51 with a median of 1.15, and 11 of 16 carry outstanding debt. Debt is denominated predominantly in USDC, with USDT0 second, held against USDe collateral within the USDe and sUSDe stablecoin E-Mode category, and since USDe is priced through the same USDT/USD feed as USDT0, the health factor of these positions tracks the USDT price relative to USDC.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 100M to 150M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 59.9% post-change cap utilization. The borrow cap is unchanged.

AUSD (Aave V3 Monad)

AUSD has reached 100.0% supply cap utilization and 45.9% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 8, 2026

All of the top suppliers hold AUSD without outstanding debt, as AUSD is not enabled as collateral on this instance. Supply is concentrated, with the largest position accounting for 51.9% of supply, the top three for 74.8%, and the top five for 82.6%.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 8, 2026

The top AUSD borrowers run health factors between 1.02 and 1.62 with a median of 1.05, and borrowing is concentrated in the largest position. syrupUSDC is the most common collateral, followed by USDe, so health factors depend on the syrupUSDC exchange rate and the price of the stablecoin collateral relative to AUSD.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 20M to 40M and the borrow cap from 18M to 32M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 50.0% post-change supply cap utilization and 25.8% post-change borrow cap utilization.

mUSD (Aave V3 Monad)

mUSD is currently at 84.1% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 8, 2026

The top mUSD borrowers run health factors between 1.01 and 1.84 with a median of 1.03, and syrupUSDC is the collateral in most positions. mUSD is priced at a fixed 1.00 USD and syrupUSDC through its exchange rate to USDC, so the health factor of these positions tracks the USDC price and the syrupUSDC exchange rate.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 25M to 40M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 52.6% post-change borrow cap utilization. The supply cap is unchanged.

Cap Reductions

On Aave V3 Monad, PT-AUSD-8OCT2026 reached its scheduled maturity on October 8, 2026. The reserve holds approximately 44.74M PT. After maturity, the PT becomes redeemable at par against the underlying. The proposed supply cap of 1 closes new deposits while existing holders retain the ability to withdraw or redeem.

USDe on Aave V3 Core sits at 57.8% supply cap utilization (404.53M / 700M), after supply declined by approximately 137M since October 6. The contraction coincided with an increase in the USDT borrow rate on the instance from approximately 4.4% to 6.8% on October 6, and the outflows came predominantly from positions holding USDe collateral against USDT debt, which repaid USDT and withdrew USDe. The proposed cap of 550M is approximately 1.36x current outstanding supply, landing at approximately 73.6% post-change cap utilization, and retains headroom for supply to return to the instance.

Aave V3 Monad PT-AUSD-8OCT2026 80,000,000 1
Aave V3 Core USDe 700,000,000 550,000,000

Aave V3 Monad AUSD 18,000,000 32,000,000

governance_posts.title: Temp Check / Discussion: Exploration of Aave Deployment on Cardano (Feasibility Study Proposal)
governance_posts.description:
Summary

This ARC proposes initiating a structured feasibility study to evaluate the potential deployment of Aave on Cardano.

The objective is to assess:

  • Technical compatibility

  • Risk framework requirements

  • Liquidity and market viability

This is the first step to determine whether further exploration is justified.

Motivation

Aave has successfully expanded across multiple EVM-compatible networks. However, the broader DeFi ecosystem remains concentrated around a single execution paradigm.

At the same time, alternative blockchain architectures have matured. Cardano represents one such environment, characterized by:

  • eUTXO-based transaction model

  • Functional programming approach to smart contracts

  • Emphasis on deterministic execution and formal methods

  • High levels of validator decentralization

Despite these properties, DeFi activity and TVL on Cardano remain relatively limited compared to other ecosystems.

This creates a potential opportunity to evaluate whether:

  • Aave could act as a foundational DeFi primitive in that environment

  • A new user and liquidity segment could be accessed

  • Architectural diversification could provide strategic value

Strategic Considerations

1. Architectural Diversification

Exploring deployment outside the EVM ecosystem may:

  • Reduce reliance on a single execution model

  • Provide exposure to alternative design trade-offs

2. Early Positioning in an Underdeveloped DeFi Market

Cardano currently lacks mature lending infrastructure at scale.
Aave could potentially:

  • Establish early presence

  • Define risk and collateral standards in a new environment

3. Emerging Collateral Opportunities (Forward-Looking)

There is ongoing development in the Cardano ecosystem around non-custodial Bitcoin interoperability, including approaches leveraging Zero-Knowledge technologies.

If successful, this could enable:

  • Use of BTC as collateral without custodial bridges

  • Reduced counterparty risk compared to wrapped assets

While early-stage, this direction may represent a differentiated collateral landscape worth monitoring.

Specification (Feasibility Study Scope)

This ARC proposes conducting a 6–8 week feasibility study covering:

Technical Assessment

  • Mapping Aave architecture to Cardano’s eUTXO model

  • Evaluation of smart contract design constraints

  • Identification of required adaptations or redesigns

Risk & Oracle Framework

  • Oracle availability and reliability

  • Liquidation mechanisms under eUTXO constraints

  • Risk parameter modeling

Market & Liquidity Analysis

  • Current DeFi activity and liquidity depth

  • Potential collateral assets

  • Incentive requirements for market bootstrapping

Ecosystem Dependencies

  • Required infrastructure (indexing, analytics, tooling)

  • Potential collaborators within the Cardano ecosystem

Implementation Considerations

Execution of the feasibility study could be carried out by:

  • Independent contributors

  • Ecosystem-aligned teams

  • External service providers

Subject to community alignment, a follow-up proposal (ARFC) would define:

  • Selected contributors

  • Detailed scope

  • Budget and timeline

Risks

Technical Complexity

  • Fundamental differences between account-based and eUTXO models

  • Potential need for partial or full redesign of components

Liquidity Fragmentation

  • Limited existing DeFi liquidity on Cardano

  • Dependence on incentives and ecosystem coordination

Opportunity Cost

  • Resource allocation vs. expanding within existing EVM ecosystems

Ecosystem Maturity

  • Tooling, oracle infrastructure, and integrations may require additional development

Cost & Funding

This ARC does not request funding.

If the community supports proceeding, a future ARFC would include:

  • A project submission on Project Catalyst to fund the initiative

Next Steps

This ARC seeks feedback from the community on:

  • Whether exploring a non-EVM deployment aligns with Aave’s strategy

  • Whether Cardano is a relevant ecosystem to evaluate

  • Whether the proposed feasibility study scope is appropriate

If there is sufficient support, the next step would be:
→ Drafting an ARFC with defined contributors, scope, and funding requirements.

Conclusion

This proposal does not advocate immediate deployment, but rather a structured evaluation of a potential strategic expansion.

The goal is to determine whether Cardano represents:

  • A viable new market for Aave

  • A meaningful diversification of execution environments

  • A forward-looking opportunity tied to emerging collateral models

Community feedback will determine whether further steps are warranted.

governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

  • Increase supply cap for PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 from 30M to 60M on Monad.

PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 (Aave V3 Monad)

PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 has reached 100.0% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 9, 2026

The top suppliers run health factors between 1.01 and 1.18 with a median of 1.03, and all of them carry outstanding debt. USDC is the dominant borrowed asset, followed by USDT0, with GHO and mUSD in a minority of positions, all held against PT collateral within the PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 stablecoin E-Mode category, and since the PT is priced through a linear discount oracle on the AUSD/USD feed, the health factor of the cohort tracks the AUSD price relative to the stablecoin debt.

Liquidity


Source: LlamaRisk, October 9, 2026

The primary trading venue is the Pendle AMM pool on Monad, which holds 3.88M in total liquidity, split 47% PT and 53% SY. Pool TVL has grown from near zero at the start of October, while the implied APY has eased from 6.0% to approximately 5.3% over the same period. The PT matures on December 17, 2026, after which it becomes redeemable at par against the underlying, so the exit at maturity does not depend on secondary market depth.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 30M to 60M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 50.0% post-change cap utilization.

Aave V3 Monad PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 30,000,000 60,000,000

governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Onboard USAT to Aave V3 Core Instance and Aave V4 Core Hub on Ethereum
governance_posts.description:
Summary

This proposal seeks to onboard USAT to the Aave V3 Core Instance and the Aave V4 Core Hub on Ethereum. Final asset configuration will be determined by the Risk Service Providers.

Motivation

USAT (Tether America USD) is a dollar stablecoin issued by Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A., a federally chartered national trust bank supervised by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). USAT is subject to the GENIUS Act and is redeemable 1:1 for U.S. dollars.

Onboarding USAT would be aligned with the DAO’s long-term objectives in several ways:

  • It introduces a stablecoin issued by a bank under federal supervision in the United States, broadening the range of regulated dollar assets available on Aave.
  • It supports demand from institutional participants seeking a stablecoin issued under the federal stablecoin framework of the United States.
  • Listing on both versions makes USAT available to Aave V3 users on Ethereum while allowing the DAO and its Service Providers to apply a configuration specific to the Aave V4 Core Hub.

Specification

This proposal adds USAT to the Aave V3 Core Instance and the Aave V4 Core Hub on Ethereum.

Token Address: 0x07041776f5007ACa2A54844F50503a18A72A8b68

Risk Parameters and final configuration will be updated by Risk Service Providers and ARFC will be updated accordingly.

Useful Links

  • USAT website
  • USAT FAQ

Disclaimer

This proposal was prepared by Aave Labs in its capacity as a contributor to the Aave ecosystem. Aave Labs has no financial relationship with Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A., Tether, or their affiliates and has not received compensation from either party in connection with this proposal.

Next Steps

  1. Gather community feedback during the ARFC stage.
  2. If the ARFC response is positive, escalate to Snapshot for offchain confirmation.
  3. Submit an AIP to Aave Governance to onboard USAT to the Aave V3 Core Instance and the Aave V4 Core Hub on Ethereum.

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V4 reserves.

Aave V4 Arc:

  • Increase slope1 for USDT on the Plus Hub from 4.50% to 4.60%.

USDC and syrupUSDC (Arc Core Hub)

syrupUSDC Supply Distribution

governance_posts.title: Core Wallet on Avalanche V3 forces unnecessary Ethereum network switch
governance_posts.description:
I am posting this here because I could not find an existing issue describing this exact Core + Avalanche V3 connection behavior.

I am using Aave V3 on Avalanche exclusively, with the Core browser extension.

There appears to be an unnecessary network-switch requirement during wallet connection.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open the Core browser extension.
  2. Set the active network to Avalanche C-Chain.
  3. Open app.aave.com.
  4. Select Avalanche Market V3.
  5. Confirm that the Aave interface is already displaying the Avalanche market.
  6. Select Connect Wallet → Core.
  7. During the connection process, Core displays:

“app.aave.com is requesting to switch your active network to Ethereum.”

  1. If I reject the Ethereum network switch, the Core/Aave wallet connection fails.
  2. If I approve the switch to Ethereum, the wallet connects successfully.
  3. When I later initiate an Aave transaction on Avalanche, I then have to switch the wallet back from Ethereum to Avalanche C-Chain.

Expected behavior

Because:

  • Aave is already set to Avalanche Market V3
  • Core is already connected to Avalanche C-Chain
  • all of my Aave activity is on Avalanche

the wallet connection should initialize directly on Avalanche C-Chain (chain ID 43114).

There should be no need to switch to Ethereum Mainnet during the initial connection and then switch back to Avalanche for the transaction.

Actual behavior

The current sequence is:

Core on Avalanche → Aave Avalanche V3 → Connect Core → forced Ethereum switch → wallet connects → initiate Avalanche transaction → switch back to Avalanche

Rejecting the Ethereum switch prevents the wallet from connecting.

Additional information

  • Wallet: Core browser extension
  • dApp: app.aave.com
  • Market: Aave V3 Avalanche
  • Intended network: Avalanche C-Chain
  • Ethereum transactions involved: None
  • ETH gas involved: None
  • Issue is reproducible consistently.

I have attached a screenshot showing Aave already on the Avalanche V3 market while Core simultaneously reports that app.aave.com is requesting a switch to Ethereum.

Could you please confirm whether this Ethereum-first connection behavior is intentional?

If not, could the wallet connection logic use the currently selected Aave market / current wallet chain when initializing the Core connection, so Avalanche users can connect directly on chain ID 43114?

governance_posts.title: [Recovery Request] Accidental Direct USDT Transfer to Aave Contract on Celo — rescueTokens Assistance Needed
governance_posts.description:
[Recovery Request] Accidental Direct USDT Transfer to Aave Contract on Celo — rescueTokens Assistance Needed

Date of Incident: June 20, 2026 Network: Celo Posted by: Andrew Kim Joseph

Summary

I previously submitted this request via email to wecare@aave.com and am following up here to ensure visibility with the broader community and relevant stakeholders.

While attempting to supply USDT to Aave on the Celo network, I mistakenly performed a direct ERC-20 token transfer to an Aave-related contract address instead of calling the appropriate supply or supplyWithPermit function. As a result, the tokens were sent directly to the contract without minting the corresponding aTokens, and the funds are now effectively locked.

I am reaching out to the Aave community and governance to inquire whether recovery is possible via the rescueTokens function, and to request that this be reviewed by the relevant parties.

Transaction Details

Field Value
Transaction Hash 0xc26b32a3bb84a8b1672337596fe7cb2906857e70426f4e494e83f07b4406e6ce
Network Celo
Token USDT
Amount 52 USDT
Sender Address 0xbA34711e2F23cCdb893FF2166f7A71f200E76b80
Destination Address 0x3E59A31363E2ad014dcbc521c4a0d5757d9f3402

What Happened

The transfer was made during an attempt to interact with the Aave protocol on Celo. Instead of invoking the supply or supplyWithPermit function on the Pool contract, a raw ERC-20 transfer was executed directly to the contract address. This resulted in the USDT arriving at the contract without triggering the deposit logic, and no aTokens were minted in return.

Recovery Request

I understand that recovery of mistakenly transferred tokens is not always possible and is subject to governance processes. However, given that:

  • The transfer occurred in the context of a direct Aave protocol interaction
  • The destination is an Aave-related contract that may hold recoverable token balances
  • The rescueTokens function exists in Aave contracts for situations such as this

I am kindly requesting that the Aave team or governance review this transaction and advise on whether a rescueTokens call is feasible and appropriate.

Additional Information

I am the owner of the sending address (0xbA34711e2F23cCdb893FF2166f7A71f200E76b80) and am happy to provide any additional verification or information required to assist with the investigation.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to any guidance the community or Aave team can offer.

— Andrew Kim Joseph andrewkimjoseph@gmail.com

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Cap and IRM Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.10.13
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Monad:

  • Increase supply cap for USDC from 250,000,000 to 350,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 225,000,000 to 315,000,000.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Reduce supply cap for USDtb from 302,000,000 to 100,000,000.
  • Reduce borrow cap for USDtb from 182,000,000 to 50,000,000.
  • Reduce supply cap for LDO from 2,000,000 to 1.
  • Reduce supply cap for tETH from 1,000 to 300.

Aave V3 Prime:

  • Reduce supply cap for tETH from 22,000 to 15,000.

Stablecoin IRM:

  • Increase Slope1 by 10 bps across V3 stablecoin reserves.

USDC (Aave V3 Monad)

USDC is currently at 90.0% supply cap utilization and 93.5% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 13, 2026

The top suppliers hold USDC without outstanding debt. Supply is concentrated, with the largest position accounting for 25.2% of supply, the top three for 51.0%, and the top five for 57.6%.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, October 13, 2026

The top USDC borrowers run health factors between 1.01 and 1.05 with a median of 1.02, and borrowing is concentrated in the largest position. Collateral behind these positions is entirely stablecoin-denominated, with USDe and syrupUSDC the largest by value, syrupUSDC the most widely held, and PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 in a minority of positions.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 250M to 350M and the borrow cap from 225M to 315M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 64.3% post-change supply cap utilization and 66.8% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Cap Reductions

  • USDtb on Aave V3 Core sits at 4.3% supply cap utilization and 5.8% borrow cap utilization, with supply down approximately 17% over the past 30 days. The asset is not enabled as collateral, so the reserve serves as a lending market only. The proposed caps of 100M supply and 50M borrow land at approximately 12.9% and 21.2% post-change cap utilization.

governance_posts.title: [Direct-to-AIP] CAPO SnapshotRatio Update Across Aave V3: October 2026
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk proposes updating the snapshotRatio to address stale snapshots and the growing drift between the CAPO upper bound and the current ratio across Aave V3. This update addresses the risk stemming from the widening spread, where, in the event of an inflation attack, collateral could become materially overpriced, potentially resulting in undercollateralized positions and bad debt for the protocol.

This follows a previous snapshot update round conducted as part of the same monitoring process, which is available here.

Upper Cap Growth

The spread between the CAPO upper bound and the current exchange rate for yield-bearing assets on Aave has widened due to a combination of high maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent values and outdated snapshots. In the event of an inflation attack, where an adversary artificially pushes the underlying exchange-rate source upward, the collateral may become overpriced. The amount of borrows that can be accumulated against this overpriced collateral is directly driven by the magnitude of the spread between the current exchange rate and the CAPO upper bound. If the spread becomes sufficiently large, the position may become undercollateralized once the exchange rate normalizes, potentially resulting in bad debt for the protocol.

The deficit trigger condition can be expressed as:

\frac{1}{(1 + \text{spread})(1+\text{LB})} < \text{maxLT}

Here, LT is chosen instead of LTV to capture the worst-case scenario, where the attacker HF approaches 1. The spread is defined as:

\text{spread} = \frac{\text{cap} - \text{currentRatio}}{\text{currentRatio}}

Running the deficit-trigger condition over every CAPO instance across Aave V3, we’ve identified the following reserves. In addition, assets projected to meet this condition within the next 30 days, based on current APY trends, have also been selected for a snapshot ratio refresh.

governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Onboard Native BTC as Collateral to Aave V4 via Babylon Trustless Bitcoin Vaults
governance_posts.description:
Author: Babylon Labs

Date: 14-10-26

Simple Summary

This proposal requests the activation of native BTC as collateral on Aave V4 via the Trustless Bitcoin Vaults (TBV) protocol. The integration deploys two new Aave V4 Spokes, the Babylon Spoke and the BTC Vault Swap Spoke, and lists native BTC as the sole collateral asset of the Babylon Spoke. The first use case is borrowing stablecoins against native BTC. Risk parameters for both Spokes will be provided by Aave’s risk service providers.

In TBV, a depositor locks BTC in a Taproot UTXO on Bitcoin Network. Redemption is governed by on-chain rules (e.g., the depositor repaid their loan) and settles directly to a Bitcoin UTXO controlled by the redeeming party. The deposited BTC is not wrapped, bridged or held by a custodian.

Following the passed Temperature Check on this integration, the ARFC extends
that scope to the integration with the Aave V4 Hub and Spoke architecture, the
BTC vault lifecycle and its trust assumptions, liquidation and arbitrage
mechanics, value accrual, and governance.

Context

Babylon

Babylon was started in 2022 by Stanford University Professor David Tse and Dr. Fisher Yu, with a vision of a Bitcoin-backed crypto economy built on trustless protocols that unlock Bitcoin’s productivity without bridges, wrappers, or custodians.

The project is best known for the Bitcoin staking protocol, which lets BTC holders stake their BTC to secure other chains and rollups to provide economic security and earn staking rewards. The protocol is fully self-custodial: BTC never leaves Bitcoin and is not held by a bridge, wrapper, or signer set. Since the protocol’s launch in August 2024, the protocol has activated over 100,000 BTC cumulatively, reached a peak TVL of 72,000 BTC, and currently holds ~40,772 BTC (approximately $3.37B) staked.

The success of Bitcoin staking demonstrated that BTC holders seek trustless and native ways to put their Bitcoin to work. This motivated the development of Trustless Bitcoin Vaults (TBV), which extends the same trustless and self-custodial principles to general DeFi participation, and is the subject of this proposal.

The Babylon project is backed by approximately $110M+ to date from a16z, Paradigm, Polychain, Hack VC and others.

Trustless Bitcoin Vaults (TBV)

Trustless Bitcoin Vaults (TBV) allows anyone to use their native bitcoins as collateral in supported on-chain applications, without transferring custody to any trusted third party.

TBV achieves this by locking BTC on Bitcoin inside a Taproot script. The conditions under which it can be moved are enforced cryptographically: redemption requires a valid zero-knowledge proof of an event on the host chain (e.g. Ethereum Mainnet), and any attempt to claim BTC without a valid proof can be challenged and stopped by an eligible challenger during a fraud-proof window. The depositor can act as a challenger themselves by operating their own vault provider, so they need not trust any third party to secure their BTC.

Spending conditions are encoded in the Taproot script and pre-authorized by all vault participants, including the depositor. The protocol itself is governed by zero-knowledge proofs through a challenge-based procedure, efficiently enabled by the BaBe protocol, and redemption is native to Bitcoin. The locked BTC moves to a recipient designated by the vault’s spending conditions, which reference events on the host chain.

TBV can be integrated with any application on any supported host chain. Ethereum is the first supported host chain and the one this integration is built on. When BTC is locked in a Taproot script, a corresponding collateral record is created on Ethereum. Each application integration builds on it, optionally via an adapter layer that exposes it through the application’s interface. For the Aave V4 integration, since Aave V4 only accepts ERC-20 tokens as collateral, the adapter contracts represent BTCVaults 1:1 as a transfer-restricted ERC-20 representation token. The full component set is detailed in Architecture Overview.

TBV is built on BaBe (eprint 2026/065), peer-reviewed cryptographic research (to appear in CCS 2026, a top security conference) developed jointly by Babylon Labs and UC Berkeley. BaBe makes SNARK proof verification on Bitcoin approximately 1000x cheaper than prior approaches, making trustless Bitcoin DeFi practical at scale.

Motivation

The Aave V4 integration with Babylon Trustless Bitcoin Vaults protocol enables onboarding of non-custodial native BTC collateral on Aave. Depositors can borrow allowed loan assets against this collateral, with no third-party custodian, signer consortium, or threshold-signature group holding the underlying BTC.

The BTC Vault Swap Spoke enables permissionless liquidation on Aave despite the underlying collateral settling natively on Bitcoin. Any liquidator can settle the position by receiving wrapped BTC for a small premium, while arbitrageurs purchase the escrowed vaults and handle the BTC-side redemption. Mechanism described in Specification.

Every escrowed BTCVault is backed by wrapped BTC borrowed from the Hub, creating new borrow demand for that asset. At launch this is WBTC, Aave’s largest BTC reserve and presently underutilized on the borrow side; the integration can use any other wrapped BTC.

Native BTC as collateral on Aave V4 also serves as a composable primitive for the broader BTC DeFi ecosystem. Other projects can build new BTC-collateralized products on top, extending Aave’s reach into BTC-native DeFi.

Specification

Architecture Overview

The TBV deployment on Ethereum consists of protocol contracts and application contracts. A BTCVault is the protocol’s core primitive, BTC locked in a UTXO on Bitcoin, secured by its pre-signed transaction graph. On Ethereum, each BTCVault is represented by a collateral record carrying its amount, its depositor, its participant set, and its lifecycle state. The protocol contracts track collateral records and enforce the vault lifecycle, from creation through activation to redemption.

The application contracts define how BTCVaults are used inside the integrated application, in this case as collateral for Aave V4 Babylon Spoke. The Aave application layer consists of the adapter contracts, the two new Spokes, and the collateral representation token. Depositors supply their BTCVaults and manage their positions through the adapter, and liquidators call it to liquidate unhealthy positions. The Babylon Spoke is a variant of the standard Aave V4 Spoke, written by Aave Labs and maintained in the Aave V4 repository (Babylon Spoke), while the BTC Vault Swap Spoke introduces custom Spoke code.

Babylon Spoke

On the Babylon Spoke, depositors borrow against native BTC, the Spoke’s only collateral asset, drawing the borrowed assets from an Aave V4 Hub.

The Spoke differs from the standard Spoke in liquidation and collateral registration only. Only the Babylon Aave V4 adapter, configured as the Spoke’s liquidation manager, can liquidate on the Spoke. The standard liquidation entry point is disabled. Each liquidation call targets one BTCVault. The adapter passes the BTCVault’s amount to the Spoke as the maximum collateral to remove, and the Spoke repays only as much debt as that amount covers at the liquidation bonus, instead of repaying toward a target health factor. The Spoke charges no liquidation fee and applies no dust threshold, so the liquidator receives all the collateral removed. A position can use only the native BTC reserve as collateral.

The Spoke exposes the same set of risk parameters as a standard Aave V4 Spoke, with values configured for this Spoke. Because the collateral token cannot be transferred, some parameters are fixed: native BTC is collateral only and non-borrowable, the liquidation fee is zero, and receiving shares on liquidation is disabled. The target health factor has been removed, as each liquidation call seizes a single BTCVault and the liquidator repeats the call until the position is healthy.

A depositor locks BTC on Bitcoin, creating a BTCVault, and supplies it through the adapter. The adapter exposes the standard position-management actions, and the liquidation (both permissionless and permissioned) entry points.

Native BTC Collateral Representation

Aave V4 accepts only ERC-20 tokens as collateral. Native BTC collateral is therefore represented by an ERC-20 token with transfer restrictions. The token is an internal accounting unit, not a BTC wrapper, it cannot be transferred between users, traded, or held anywhere outside the integration.

The token has 8 decimals, matching Bitcoin’s satoshi denomination. Transfers are allowed only between the integration’s Aave contracts, a fixed allowlist made up of the Aave V4 Hub, the adapter contract, and the per-user position proxy contracts that hold each depositor’s position.

There are no risk parameters to configure for this token. The token contract is not upgradeable and has no admin. Its decimals, transfer restrictions, and the Hub and adapter addresses are set at deployment and cannot be changed.

Mint and burn are restricted to the adapter contract. The token is minted at BTCVault activation, directly into the depositor’s position, and burned when a vault leaves a position, whether withdrawn by the depositor or seized in liquidation. No other mint or burn path exists. By design, total supply equals the BTC locked in active positions.

BTC Vault Swap Spoke

A custom Spoke for post-liquidation BTC collateral settlement.

When a position is liquidated by a permissionless liquidator, the liquidator swaps the acquired BTCVaults through this Spoke for wrapped BTC, at the oracle rate minus a sell discount. The wrapped BTC is a BTC-denominated ERC-20 fixed when the Spoke is deployed, WBTC at launch. It is drawn from an Aave V4 Hub and held as interest-accruing debt against the escrowed BTCVaults. Arbitrageurs, a permissioned set with redemption rights, later buy individual escrowed BTCVaults by repaying that debt (principal plus accrued interest) and redeem the BTC on Bitcoin.

The Spoke exists because BTC redemption is restricted to pre-committed actors in each BTCVault’s Taproot script and takes multiple days through the claim challenge window. Decoupling liquidation timing from BTC redemption lets permissionless liquidators settle in wrapped BTC immediately while arbitrageurs handle redemption on Bitcoin’s timeline.

The BTC Vault Swap Spoke moves Hub funds in two ways. The first is the wrapped BTC draw and repayment described above. The second is the deficit path, used when an escrowed BTCVault’s value no longer covers its Hub debt. The BTCVault stays purchasable at its current value. The arbitrageur repays the Hub debt, capped at the BTCVault’s value less a reserved arbitrageur margin. Any shortfall is reported to the Hub as a deficit in the same transaction.

The BTC Vault Swap Spoke has 3 configurable parameters: the sell discount, the minimum profit reserved for the arbitrageur, and the fee recipient.

Governance, Control & Pause States

Both Spokes (the Babylon Spoke and the BTC Vault Swap Spoke) are governed by Aave DAO. Aave DAO lists the collateral asset and the borrowable assets, and sets the Spoke configuration parameters, including supply and borrow caps, interest rate strategy, liquidation parameters, and oracle configuration. It can also freeze or pause each listed asset individually, where freezing stops new supply and borrowing while pausing stops all activity for that asset. Any Hub used for drawing liquidity for these Spokes will also be governed by Aave DAO. A separate role for configuring the BTC Vault Swap Spoke is held by a 2-of-3 multisig of Llama Risk, Babylon Labs, and Aave Labs.

The Babylon TBV contracts are governed by Babylon governance representatives. They manage the TBV protocol configuration and the actor sets, and hold pause and freeze controls over the TBV contracts. A freeze blocks new vault creations and new borrows, while all exit paths keep working. A pause additionally stops the exit paths and is reserved for emergencies. All governance actions on the TBV contracts execute through a public timelock with advance on-chain notice.

Vault Lifecycle & Position Management

Vault Creation

The TBV protocol is trustless. BTCVault creation and redemption need a set of actors that coordinate with each other. The protocol defines three types of actors.

  • Vault Provider. An infrastructure operator appointed by the depositor. It sets up and redeems the BTCVault for that depositor and challenges fraudulent claims. The depositor can run it themselves.
  • Application Vault Keepers. An application-specific set of actors with claim and challenge rights over that application’s BTCVaults. On Aave V4, they claim BTCVaults that have been liquidated and act as the arbitrageurs.
  • Universal Challengers. A global set of actors. They can challenge bad claims on any BTCVault, across every application.

The depositor locks BTC in a Taproot output on Bitcoin and submits a creation request on Ethereum. The vault provider, every application vault keeper, and every universal challenger must acknowledge the request and pre-sign the vault’s transaction graph, the fixed set of Bitcoin transactions through which the locked BTC can ever move. Acknowledgments are given only after the locked BTC is confirmed on Bitcoin. By design, nothing outside the pre-signed graph can spend the vault.

Once all acknowledgments are in, the depositor activates the vault by revealing a secret on Ethereum. If the depositor does not activate, or any actor fails to acknowledge, the request expires and the depositor reclaims the locked BTC unilaterally through a timelocked refund. By design, collateral can never exist without locked BTC behind it. On activation, the BTCVault enters the depositor’s Aave position, and from there the position is managed through the adapter.

Position Management

Every position action goes through the adapter. The depositor never interacts with the Babylon Spoke directly.

Borrowing and repaying follow standard Aave mechanics. On top of Aave interest, the adapter can charge a Babylon interest fee, a percentage of the borrower’s base Aave interest, collected on repayment. Collateral handling is custom, tailored to BTCVaults. A position can hold several BTCVaults. Each one is a single locked Bitcoin UTXO, so collateral moves in whole BTCVaults and never in part. The Babylon Spoke sees only the position’s total collateral amount, while the adapter tracks which BTCVaults make it up. The depositor adds collateral by activating additional BTCVaults into the position and withdraws whole BTCVaults while the position’s health factor stays at or above liquidation threshold. A borrower with multiple BTCVaults can set the order in which a liquidation seizes them.

Vault Redemption

A BTCVault is redeemed when application logic on Ethereum releases it. In the Aave V4 integration this happens in two cases. The borrower withdraws any subset of their BTCVaults while the position stays healthy, or the vault is liquidated and leaves through the liquidation flow. The application contracts define and enforce these rules on Ethereum. Each redemption emits an event naming the BTC keys authorized to claim the vault on Bitcoin.

The claim settles on Bitcoin. Only actors pre-committed in the vault’s Taproot script can claim, and the depositor is always one of them. The authorized claimer posts a Claim backed by a zero-knowledge proof of the Ethereum redemption event. If the proof is invalid, any challenger can stop the Claim during the claim challenge window. Challengers are all of the vault’s participants, the vault provider, every application vault keeper, and every universal challenger. By design, a challenge cannot block a valid claim. After the window passes, the BTC settles to the authorized key. The full timeline from redemption to settlement is multiple days, set by the claim challenge window.

Liquidation

Once a position’s health factor drops below liquidation threshold, anyone can liquidate it through the adapter, one BTCVault at a time. The adapter seizes the first BTCVault in the order the borrower set in advance. The liquidator repays the position’s debt asset. The collateral the Spoke removes is priced at the standard Aave liquidation bonus for the position’s health factor at entry. The Spoke stops once the collateral owed for the repaid debt reaches the BTCVault’s amount. The adapter refunds any repayment input the Spoke did not spend. A position holding several BTCVaults is liquidated through repeated calls. Each call checks the health factor again.

Liquidation always seizes whole BTCVaults. If the borrower’s entire debt is repaid before the BTCVault’s amount is consumed, the liquidator still receives the whole BTCVault and pays the borrower for the remainder in wrapped BTC (WBTC at launch) at the same liquidation-bonus discount. The borrower therefore receives that portion as discounted wrapped BTC instead of native BTC. The liquidator must hold the wrapped BTC and sets a cap on the total it can be charged.

Liquidation runs through two paths (permissioned and permissionless). In the permissioned path, an application vault keeper, which holds redemption rights over the vault, liquidates the position and redeems the seized BTCVault to its own BTC key. No external liquidity is involved.

In the permissionless path, anyone can liquidate. Because redemption is restricted to the pre-committed actors in each BTCVault’s Taproot script, these liquidators cannot redeem the BTCVaults they seize, so the integration introduces liquidation liquidity providers. A venue swaps the seized BTCVaults for a fungible asset immediately, instead of after the multi-day Bitcoin settlement.

The BTC Vault Swap Spoke is the first such venue. It purchases the seized BTCVaults from the liquidator for wrapped BTC drawn as debt from an Aave V4 Hub in the same transaction and holds them in escrow for the arbitrageurs to buy and redeem, as described in Architecture Overview. Additional venues can be added if scale requires.

Aave DAO Value Accrual

On the Babylon Spoke, borrowers pay standard borrow interest on every asset drawn from the Hub, exactly as on any other Spoke. On the BTC Vault Swap Spoke, escrowed BTCVaults accrue wrapped BTC borrow interest to the Hub until an arbitrageur repays the draw. This adds borrow demand on whichever wrapped BTC the integration uses, WBTC at launch, Aave’s largest wrapped BTC reserve and presently underutilized on the borrow side.

Native BTC as collateral on Aave V4 also serves as a composable primitive for the broader BTC DeFi ecosystem. Other projects can build new BTC-collateralized products on top, extending Aave’s reach into BTC-native DeFi.

Revenue Sharing

This proposal includes revenue sharing between Aave DAO and Babylon Foundation.
Babylon Foundation is responsible for the incentive arrangements supporting the
integration, such as borrower incentives and strategic integrations. These do
not guarantee borrower demand, revenue, token purchases or returns.

Revenue sharing applies only to Qualifying Revenue, the protocol-level fees
listed below, not all interest paid by borrowers:

  • The Aave Hub’s Liquidity Fee on interest paid by Babylon Spoke borrowers.
  • Liquidation fees charged through the adapter and the BTC Vault Swap Spoke.

The first $500,000 of Qualifying Revenue in each year from launch goes entirely
to Aave DAO. Above that, each band’s split applies only to the revenue within
that band, with distributions made monthly.

The token purchase allocation funds open-market purchases of AAVE (85%) and
BABY (15%), with purchased tokens allocated equally to Aave DAO and
Babylon Foundation.

Annual revenue band Aave DAO Babylon Token purchase allocation
First $500,000 100% 0% 0%
$500,000–$2 million 78% 18% 4%
$2 million–$4 million 72.5% 22.5% 5%
$4 million–$6 million 67% 27% 6%
Above $6 million 61.5% 31.5% 7%

Audits & Formal Verification

Security audit engagements have been completed across five components, the btc-vault, the vault provers, the smart contracts, the web services, and BaBe. Six firms were engaged, with overlapping scopes so that every component is covered by at least two independent reviews. Coinspect additionally performed a pre-audit of the full protocol before the main engagements. Runtime Verification performed formal verification of the smart contracts. Babylon is running a re-audit of the finalized changes before mainnet deployment, carried out by Coinspect, ABDK and Zellic. The follow-up reports will be shared once finalized.

Firm Scope
Coinspect Pre-audit (full protocol) + btc-vault, vault provers, smart contracts, web services audit
Sherlock btc-vault, vault provers, smart contracts, web services, BaBe
Zellic btc-vault, smart contracts
ABDK Vault provers, smart contract cryptography, BaBe (paper and implementation)
ZK Security BaBe
Runtime Verification Formal verification of the smart contracts

Next Steps

  1. Seek community feedback and risk analysis
  2. If community consensus is reached, raise to Snapshot.
  3. If the Snapshot outcome is positive, submit an AIP, with full risk parameters included, for on-chain governance approval.

Babylon Labs is the author of this proposal. We have not been compensated by any third party to publish it.

This ARFC has been prepared solely to facilitate community discussion.
